The Tejobindu Upaniṣad.
"May He protect us both"—thus [ends] the peace invocation.
Chapter One.
The nature of the point of light is without distinction;
it is the supreme meditation on the point of light, abiding in the heart of the Soul of the Universe—
that which is atomic, pertaining to Śambhu, peaceful, and both gross, subtle, and supreme.
Abounding in hardship, difficult to propitiate, hard to behold, liberated, and immutable—that meditation is difficult to attain even for sages and wise men. || 2 ||
I am that Brahman, the indivisible single essence of pure consciousness, wherein even the notion of "mere consciousness" is immediately sublated.

Indeed, this *Tejobindu Upaniṣad*, which is a division of the *Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda*, unfolds here for the purpose of attaining *kaivalya*—the state of liberation while in the body—characterized by abiding in the nature of partless, indivisible bliss and pure consciousness, established through the negation of all that is other than one's own self. Its introductory context and so forth are similar to those of the *Kaṭhavallī* and other Upaniṣads. Now begins a commentary on this *Tejobindu Upaniṣad*, which illuminates the experience of Brahman alone, based on its brief text.

(p. 46) The narrative consisting of the questions and answers of Śiva, Skanda, Ṛbhu, and Nidāgha, which is about to be told, is intended for the praise of *vidyā* (knowledge). Here, at the outset, in the first chapter, without the formal structure of question and answer, the *Śruti* itself instructs the qualified aspirants on the reality of the non-dual Brahman (*nirviśeṣabrahmatattva*), which is established through the practice of the fifteen-limbed yoga (*pañcadaśāṅgayoga*). "Tejobindu... [The text begins]. For those sages (*munayaḥ*) who desire to contemplate the true nature of their own Self, and for those wise ones (*manīṣiṇaḥ*) whose intellect is fixed on the meditation on non-dual Brahman—for them, I shall explain that supreme meditation (*dhyāna*) concerning that [Brahman], which is established by the negation (*apahnava*) of the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its effects, which are other than oneself, and which is the very nature of the *tejobindu* (the point of light), the non-correlative (*niṣpratiyogika*) Self alone. This is the implied sense. What is the nature of that which is to be meditated upon? To this it says: "Viśva... The universe (*viśva*) is that which ignorant people believe exists as something separate from themselves; it is the aggregate of one's own ignorance and its effects. That whose body (*ātman*) is this universe is the "Self of the Universe" (*viśvātmā*), the Virāṭ. It resides within the heart-lotus of that [Virāṭ] as the illuminator of its thousands of mental modifications. How can the groundless state of ignorance remain? To this it says: "Aṇu... It is called *aṇuva* because it carries (*vahati*) the entire essence of the state of ignorance—whether in the form of Ādikūrma and others, as the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*), or as the substrate of all (*sarvādhiṣṭhāna*)—in a subtle manner. It is "atomic" (*aṇutva*) because it is limited in relation to itself. It is "Śambhu" because peace (*śam*) arises from it; it is the inward-facing Self (*pratyak*), for the bliss pertaining to it is dependent upon it. Its true nature is non-dual Brahman, which is "Śāmbhava. In reality, it is the cessation of all conceptualizations such as the universe and Virāṭ. When, from the perspective of the ignorant, there arises the conceptualization of the gross and subtle world, that which is the locus of both superimposition (*āropa*) and negation (*apavāda*) is distinct from and beyond that gross and subtle world. By the word "and" (*ca*), its distinction even from the fourth state (*turya*) is indicated. Because it cannot be grasped through the perception of the ignorant, it is full of suffering, difficult to propitiate, and difficult to behold. From the perspective of the knower of the Self, it is free from all such conceptualizations; therefore, it is "imperishable" (*avyaya*), since the delusion of anything other than the Self—which causes decay—is impossible. Without the grace of the *Śruti* and the teacher, its true nature or the meditation upon it is difficult to attain by one's own effort; however, through the grace of the *Śruti* and the teacher, it is indeed easy to understand. || 2 ||
The means for attaining the realization of non-differentiated Brahman are:
one who is moderate in diet, who has conquered anger, conquered attachment, and conquered the senses;
who is free from the pairs of opposites, free from egoism, free from desire, and free from possessiveness. || 3 ||
Those who engage with the unapproachable while their minds are intent on approaching the approachable find the three [vowels] in the mouth; he whose abode is threefold is called the *haṃsa*. (4)
Know this to be the supreme secret; indeed, free from sloth and without support, the subtle digit in the form of the moon is the highest state of Viṣṇu.

The realization of that [Truth] indeed occurs for those of the highest capacity. Regarding how those of dull or middling capacity may attain that realization, he teaches the means—beginning with the word *yata*. O world of those who lack self-knowledge (*svājñaloka*), if you desire to attain your own state through the self-knowledge arising from my instruction, then, having become endowed with the means taught by me, you shall go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu; such is the syntactical connection.
"Two parts of food, and a third part of water—one should leave the fourth part remaining for the movement of the vital air (*vāyu*)."

Thus, since your food is restricted, you must first become one whose food is regulated, for according to the scripture: "When food is pure, the essence [of being] becomes pure," and so forth. You must become one who has conquered anger—that anger which arises from desire and loss. You must become one who has conquered attachment and the group of senses—that is, one by whom attachment to the objects of the senses as imagined by one's own mind has been conquered. You must become free from dualities—that is, one from whom the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat have departed. You must become free from egoism—that is, one from whom the sense of "I" regarding the three bodies has departed. You must become free from longing—that is, one from whom the desire (*āśīḥ*) to consume enjoyments other than oneself has departed. You must become one without possessions—that is, one by whom the acquisition of anything other than the requisites suitable for maintaining mere life is not grasped. He says, "Having approached," etc., meaning: "Meditate first upon that state which the partial knowers of the Self attain. Those who, with minds conditioned by identification with those states, do not go toward the universe, Virāṭ, Otr, and so forth—which are accessible only to the ignorant and serve as the locus for the superimposition of the plane of their own ignorance—are called "those who do not go where they should go" (*agamyāgamakartāraḥ*). Those whose minds do not engage in going toward the plane of their own ignorance and its effects, which are accessible to the vision of the ignorant, are indeed "those whose minds do not go where they should go" (*gamyāgamanamānasāḥ*).

(48) Those who have taken refuge in the variegated Brahman (*śabalabrahma*) and are partial knowers of themselves—knowing that the waking state resides in the eye, as established by the scripture stating "The Viśva [aspect] is in the opening of the right eye"—they perceive, through their own non-difference, the three forms each (Viśva-Viśva, etc., Virāṭ-Virāṭ, etc., and Otr-Otra, etc. belonging to the waking-waking and other states, by virtue of being the substratum of the individual (*vyaṣṭi*), the collective (*samaṣṭi*), and the unity of both; and by the word "and" (*ca*), they also perceive the respective forms of the *turya* (the fourth). Thus, he who possesses these three abodes is called the *Tridhāma Haṃsa*. By his own knowledge, he destroys (*han*) the self of those who worship him; thus, the meaning is that the Supreme Lord is the *Haṃsa*. Having meditated upon this very *Haṃsa* as "I am He" (*so'ham*), you—being one whose lassitude (*tandrī*) and weariness (*jāmitā*) have been cast away (*astā-tandrī*)—become supportless (*nirāśraya*) due to the absence of any support other than your own Self. Know, understand, that which I speak of as the secret (*guhyatamam*) Brahman: because it is the substratum for the sublation of everything, and because it cannot be spoken to one who lacks the qualification for the conceptualization of waking-waking and so forth, it remains as nothing but its own nature when the state of being a substratum dependent on a superstratum has ceased. What is that? He says: "Soma... Accompanied by *Umā*, which is one's own innate wisdom (*svavidyā*), the digit (*kalā*) known by the perfect knowledge of the sages is the digit in the form of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). It is subtle due to its lack of distinction. That very digit, when there is the possibility of the pervaded as imagined by the vision of the ignorant, becomes the pervader; yet, through the vision of the perfectly wise, the pervaded and the pervader are negated, and what remains is the supreme, non-relative, unsurpassed state. Because it is reached (*padyate*) as that alone, it is the "foot" (*padam*); the meaning is that only one's own nature remains. (5)
Since the states such as possessing distinctions belong only to an external object,

[the Self is] three-faced, consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa), the locus of the three realms (tridhātu), yet devoid of form; it is immovable, free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa), formless, and without support.
The state free from limiting adjuncts, beyond the reach of speech and mind, the essential nature graspable through existence, uncomposite, and the infallible ground.
Beyond manifold bliss, difficult to behold, liberated, and imperishable; thus freed from all thought, it is eternal, constant, and infallible. (8)
That is Brahman; that is the supreme self (adhyātma); that is the ultimate goal of Viṣṇu;
it is the inconceivable, pure consciousness, the supreme ether that abides.
It is non-empty, yet its nature is emptiness; it abides in the heart as that which transcends emptiness.
There is neither meditation, nor a meditator, nor an object of meditation, and yet it is indeed the very object of meditation.
They do not know anything as being other than empty, nor as other, nor as the highest other;
they know it neither as inconceivable nor as unawakened, nor as real, nor as the supreme.
Neither the gods nor others know that which is fully realized by the sages:
greed, delusion, fear, pride, desire, anger, and sin.
Cold and heat, hunger and thirst, conceptualization and discursive thought, pride in the lineage of Brahmins, and the accumulation of the knots of bondage—none of these [exist]. 13.
There is neither fear nor pleasure, nor pain, nor likewise honor or dishonor;
that which is completely free from these states is Brahman—that is the supreme Brahman.

He says "the three-faced one" (*trivaktram*) to indicate that this very [Reality] appears as if it assumes, through the perspective of its own ignorance (*svājñā*), the state of having distinctions (*saviśeṣatā*) and, in relation to that, the state of being without distinctions (*nirviśeṣatā*); yet from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), it remains non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) and devoid of any counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika*). It is "three-faced" by way of the divisions of Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña; "three-stringed" (*triguṇam*) by way of the divisions of Virāṭ, Sūtra, and so forth; and a "station" (*sthānam*) because it is the goal to be attained by the liberated. It is "three-layered" (*tridhātum*) by way of the divisions of the Permitter, the Authorizer, and the Consenter, or by way of the divisions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa. In reality, however, it is devoid of the aforementioned nature of the three faces and so on, due to the total absence of any support for movement, conceptualization, or form.

(50) It is motionless (*niścalam*), free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpam*), formless (*nirākāram*), and without support (*nirāśrayam*). (6) It is devoid of limiting adjuncts (*upādhirahitam*) because it is itself without adjuncts. Its "state" (*sthānam*) has already been explained. It is the "object" (*gocaram*) because it transcends speech and mind as the Fourth State (*turīya*). It is "self-nature" (*svabhāvam*) because it exists by itself alone. It is to be correctly grasped as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpeṇa*) because it is pure Being (*sanmātratvāt*). It is "non-composite" (*asaṃghātam*) because it is outside the collection of the senses. It is "unfallen from its own nature" (*svasvabhāvādacyutam*). (7) It is "not manifold-bliss" (*anānānandanaḥ*) because the individual soul (*jīvaḥ*) is not that; it is the Witness (*sākṣī*). It has transcended even that state. The three terms "difficult to perceive," "liberated," and "immutable" (*duṣprekṣyaṃ muktamavyayam*) have been explained. It should always be contemplated as immutable. Should there arise the possibility of it being something qualified by such contemplation, it is "thus liberated" (*evaṃvinirmuktam*), because it cannot be conceived by anyone. It is "eternal" (*śāśvatam*) because the non-eternal universe does not exist. It is "constant" (*dhruvam*) because of the disappearance of unstable *māyā*. It is "unfallen" (*acyutam*) because there is no falling away in any way whatsoever. (8) That which is thus is the essential nature of Brahman. Because it exists as the inner self (*pratyagrūpeṇa*) with respect to the Virāj, who is the Self of all, it is "pertaining to the self" (*adhyātmam*). That very same thing is also the essential nature of Viṣṇu. That alone is the "highest goal" (*tatparāyaṇam*) because it is Nārāyaṇa, the one to be attained by the liberated. It is "inconceivable" (*acintyam*) as a non-differentiated Self, due to the absence of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). [Regarding the phrase] "consisting of consciousness as its Self" (*cinmayātmānam*): the change of case ending and gender is Vedic (*chāndasa*), meaning "having consciousness as its essence" (*cinmayātmakam*). It is "space" (*vyoma*) because it is the space of consciousness (*cidākāśatvāt*). "Supreme" (*paramam*) has been explained. It is "established" (*sthitam*) because it is pure existence (*sattāmātratvāt*). (9) Therefore, it is "not empty" (*aśūnyam*). Because it is full, it is the state of emptiness regarding anything other than itself. The word "but" (*tu*) is for the sake of emphasis. It has transcended even that which has reached the state of emptiness—other than itself—because it is without a counter-correlative (*niṣpratiyogikatvāt*). It resides in the heart in the form of the inner witness (*pratyagādi*). Since there would be a triad (*tripuṭī*) if it were merely the inner witness, he says: "Not. There is no meditation (*dhyānam*) apart from itself, nor a meditator (*dhyātā*), nor an object of meditation (*dhyeyaḥ*). Yet, because nothing remains but itself, it is indeed the object of meditation. (10) If everything were to follow as being apart from itself, then nothing would exist. If it did exist, then there would be an emptiness beyond itself. Therefore, there is nothing higher (*param*). Even that which is "higher" in relation to something else is not itself [independent]. Because it is impossible to think of, know, or see it as separate from itself, the sages (*munayaḥ*) know it as inconceivable and unawakened; they do not know it as the "Real" (*satyam*) or the "Higher" (*param*). That which is the "Higher" and "beyond" is what the sages have joined with and determined. Even the gods, though possessed of subtle intellects, do not know that there is anything beyond that. In the passage beginning with "greed" (*lobham*), a change of gender should be understood. Indeed, there are no mental modifications (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) such as greed or delusion; no pairs of opposites (*dvandva*) such as cold and heat; no six waves (*ṣaḍūrmayaḥ*) such as hunger and thirst; no mental functions (*mānasavṛtti*) such as volition and doubt; no pride (*darpa*) such as "I am born into a lineage starting with Brahmā"; no accumulation of knots (*granthi-saṃcaya*) such as bondage and liberation; nor any states of honor or dishonor. That which is entirely free from all these states—
That Brahman is established through the negation of the generality that is distinct from itself; the meaning is that that supreme Brahman remains as its own self alone. || 12–14 ||
The fifteen-limbed yoga is the means for realizing the Supreme Brahman:

restraint (yama), observance (niyama), renunciation (tyāga), silence (mauna), and [proper] place and time; posture (āsana), the root-lock (mūlabandha), equilibrium of the body, and the steadiness of vision. || 15 ||

Control of the vital breath (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation on the self (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi) are indeed declared to be the limbs [of yoga] in their proper sequence. (16)

If Brahman is thus devoid of any counter-correlate (niṣpratiyogika), then one might suspect a lack of means for its realization. Anticipating this, if you have a desire to realize It, then the fifteen-limbed yoga is taught as the means for that realization—beginning with "Yama and Niyama. In this way, the fifteen limbs of yoga are briefly stated. (Verses 15–16)

Through the knowledge that all the characteristics of the fifteen components are indeed Brahman, the restraint of the collection of senses is proclaimed as "Yama"; this should be practiced again and again. (17)
A continuous flow of the same kind and the exclusion of what is dissimilar—this is indeed the rule of supreme bliss, which is practiced by the wise through self-restraint. (18)
Renunciation consists in the perception of the Self as Being-Consciousness amidst the nature of phenomenal expansion;
for the renunciation of the great is worthy of worship and bestows immediate liberation. (19)
Since words turn back from it along with the mind without reaching it—that silence which is to be realized by yogis—let that state always be [the goal] for the dull-witted as well. 20.
Since words turn back from it, by whom can that be spoken?
Even if the phenomenal world were to be spoken of, it too is devoid of sound. (21)
Or rather, that silence which is known as the "innate" (sahaja) may be all-encompassing;
however, silence consisting merely of not speaking is unfit for those who speak of Brahman, for it is the silence of children.
That place where no person is found in the beginning, the end, or the middle, and which is perpetually pervaded by that [Reality], is known as a secluded place (vijana). || 23 ||
The conceptualization of all beings, beginning with Brahmā, from the moment of a blink of an eye, is indeed designated by the word "time" (kāla), which is non-dual and of unbroken bliss. (24)
One should know that to be a true seat (āsana) in which the constant contemplation of Brahman occurs with ease; any other is a destroyer of happiness. (25)
For the sake of accomplishment, the non-dual foundation of the universe, beginning with all beings, exists;
the perfected ones (siddhas) have attained accomplishment within it, and thus it is called their Siddhāsana.

That which is the root of all worlds, that which is the root of the bondage of the mind—this root-binding (mūlabandha) should always be practiced; it is suitable for those who are royal yogins (rājayogins).
One should know the evenness of the limbs; when [the mind] is in the even Brahman, it dissolves there.
Otherwise, there is no such evenness, and there is no straightness, like a withered tree.
Having made one's vision consist of knowledge, one should behold the world as consisting of Brahman;
that vision is supremely noble, not the gazing at the tip of the nose.
p. 53) Where there may be the cessation of the seer, the seeing, and the seen—there alone the vision should be directed; it is not that which looks at the tip of the nose. (30)
Because all things, beginning with the mind, are meditated upon as being Brahman itself, the cessation of all mental fluctuations is called *prāṇāyāma*. (31)
The negation of conceptual proliferation (prapañca) is declared to be that which is called exhalation (recaka);
the mental state [realizing] "I am indeed Brahman" is said to be inhalation (pūraka). (32)
Therefore, the steadiness of that state is *kumbhaka*, the restraint of breath;
this is for the awakened, while for the ignorant it is merely the oppression of the nose. (33)

Having perceived the nature of the self within sense objects, that which delights the mind of the mental faculty is to be known as withdrawal (pratyāhāra); it should be practiced again and again. (34)
Wherever the mind goes, because of the vision of Brahman there, the fixing [of the mind] by means of the mind is considered that supreme concentration (dhāraṇā). || 35 ||
The state of abiding in the conviction "I am indeed Brahman," characterized by true delight and objectlessness, is renowned by the term *dhyāna*; it bestows supreme bliss. (36)
Furthermore, when the mental modification is free from transformation and takes the form of Brahman, the complete forgetting of that very modification is designated as Samādhi. (37)

The *Śruti* itself explains, in due order, the fifteen limbs that constitute the aphorism (*sūtra*). Therein, it states the meaning of the word "restraint" (*yama*) as "all. The meaning is that restraint is the state of Brahman within the entire collection of instruments (*karaṇagrāma*). It states the meaning of the word "observance" (*niyama*) as "of one's own kind," and so forth.

(54) The mental modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of undivided pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and so forth is of the same class (*sajātīya*); the modification consisting of pots, cloths, and so forth is of a different class (*vijātīya*). (18) He explains the word "renunciation" (*tyāga*): "Renunciation... The meaning is that the vision of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*) devours the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) of unreality and the like. (19) He reveals the meaning of the word "silence" (*mauna*): "Because... An alternative view is given: "of speech. In the first view, silence is said to be the cessation of the respective functions of the sense organs such as speech by those who are inert (*jaḍa*). In the second view, however, because it is impossible to define [the Self] as being either existent or non-existent in relation to anything other than itself—which is ultimately non-dual—[true silence is not the mere stopping of speech]. The silence spoken of in the first definition belongs to children, not to the knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*). (20–22) He explains the meaning of the word "place" (*deśa*): "In the beginning... The meaning is that such a place is Brahman alone. (23) He states the meaning of the word "time" (*kalā*): "Imagination... That which is imagined through the twinkling of the eye of ignorance, and whose substratum is Brahman—that is what is denoted by the word "time. (24) He clarifies the meaning of the word "posture" (*āsana*): "With ease... A comfortable posture conducive to meditation is the "Siddhāsana," which grants success; it does not mean merely sitting straight like a pillar. (25–26) He makes manifest the nature of the "root-lock" (*mūlabandha*): "That which... Brahman, the cause of all, is indeed the root-lock; it is not the contraction of the body and so forth. This is suitable for *rājayogins*, not for *haṭhayogins*. (27) He states the meaning of the word "equality of the body" (*dehasāmya*): "Of the limbs... Equality is the state of dissolution of the gross and other bodies into the equal Brahman; it is not simply straightness like a pillar. (28) He describes the nature of "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*): "Vision... The vision of one ignorant of oneself sees the world as separate from oneself. The vision of the knower of the Self, which perceives the substratum of all, is the vision of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), knowing Brahman alone. Therefore, the vision of one's own self alone should be maintained in Brahman, which is established through the negation of the triad of seer, seeing, and seen. (29–30) He describes the nature of the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) of the wise, accompanied by exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*): "Mind, etc... The contemplation that "everything is Brahman" is *prāṇāyāma*. The realization that "the world separate from oneself does not exist" is the function of exhalation (*recaka*). The thought "I am that very [Brahman]" is the function of inhalation (*pūraka*). The steadiness of that function is the function of retention (*kumbhaka*). For the knowers of the Self, it is thus; for the ignorant, the result is merely the oppression of the nose. (31–33) He describes the nature of "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*): "In objects... Withdrawing the senses from objects and viewing all objects as Brahman is *pratyāhāra*. (34) He describes the nature of "concentration" (*dhāraṇā*): "Where... The meaning is that Brahman is the locus where the movement of the mind occurs. (35) He defines "meditation" (*dhyāna*): "Brahman... Meditation is the contemplation of Brahman without any external support (*nirālamba*). (36) He describes the nature of "absorption" (*samādhi*): "Changeless... A mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of the undivided whole is *savikalpa*; the non-recollection of that modification is *nirvikalpa-samādhi*. (37)
Through the practice of yoga, one should thoroughly cultivate this abode of Brahman, which is of the nature of bliss,
until the true selfhood of the person spontaneously arises within the focal point in an instant. (38)
Then, liberated from all means of accomplishment, he becomes a perfected king of yogis;
her own true nature becomes the object of his mind and speech. (39)
The seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) should practice this very yoga of fifteen limbs until he abides as nothing but Brahman; then he becomes Brahman itself—thus it is said: "This... (verses 38–39).
The pacification of obstacles to concentration:
indeed, when concentration is being practiced, obstacles come forth by force—namely, a lack of sustained application, laziness, and a longing for sensual enjoyments. (40)
Lassitude, darkness, distraction, heat, perspiration, and emptiness—indeed, such a multitude of obstacles must be abandoned by those who are experts in Brahman. (41)
For through the state of existence there is existence; through the state of emptiness there is emptiness;
and through the state of Brahman there is fullness. Therefore, one should practice that fullness.

Raising the doubt as to how non-conceptual samādhi (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) can arise when obstacles to samādhi—such as the lack of continuous application (*anusaṃdhāna*)—are present, [the author] states, "In samādhi," etc., to show that the complete, undivided samādhi arises through the pacification of those obstacles. The meaning is this: for one engaged in the practice of samādhi, when a multitude of obstacles—consisting of occasional lapses into non-application and other such void mental states (*śūnya-vṛtti*)—arise either individually or simultaneously, one should uproot that entire mass of obstacles by means of methods such as continuous application; then, one should practice one's own full state of being through the undivided mental mode (*akhaṇḍākāra-vṛtti*) of "I am indeed Brahman. (Verses 40–42)
(56) Through meditative absorption (samādhi), one attains the state of pure Brahman:
"Those men who, having abandoned this supreme, purifying mode called Brahman, live in vain, are equal to beasts. (43)
But those who understand their livelihood and, having understood it, truly increase it—they are indeed virtuous men, blessed, and worthy of worship throughout the three worlds. || 44 ||
Those whose conduct is even, mature, and fully ripened—
they alone have attained the state of true Brahmanhood, and not others who are merely talkers of words.
Those who are skilled in the discourse of Brahman, yet devoid of right conduct and full of passion, surely come and go again due to their ignorance. (46)
They do not remain for even half a moment without the functioning of knowledge;
they remain just as Brahmā and the others, Sanaka and the others, and Śuka and the others do.
That for which the effect is indeed the cause, its causality arises;
however, from the perspective of inquiry, that causality perishes in reality when the effect is absent. (48)
Now, when the object is pure and indeed beyond the range of words, the knowledge of mental modification (vṛttijñāna) arises for those of pure mind; it is superior to that.
Having cultivated through intense yoga that object which consists of certainty, one should lead the visible into invisibility and contemplate it in the form of Brahman. (50)
The wise man should always abide in bliss with a consciousness filled with the essence of pure awareness. || 51 ||
Thus [it is said].

(p. 57) He refutes those for whom the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of Brahman is rare: "Those who... (43). Only those possessing the mental modification in the form of the indivisible (*akhaṇḍākāra*) reach the state of Brahman; those contrary to that resort to *saṃsāra*. Since this is so, he says "But those who... (44–47), meaning that those desiring the state of Brahman, like Śrī Śuka, Sanaka, and others, should practice *samādhi* alone. Because the mental modification in the form of the indivisible is produced by practice, practice is the cause and the mental modification in the form of the indivisible is the effect. Raising the doubt—"Since that [modification] is produced, it is non-eternal; how can one attain the eternal Brahman through it?"—he says "The cause... (48). For one who speaks thus, the very cause called practice becomes the effect. By stating that the effect is something produced, and by the reasoning of the dependent scripture (*sāpekṣa-śruti*) which says "if there is an effect," the cause itself would perish when the effect is absent. The sense is this: when both the locus of the superimposition and its effects—the state of one's own ignorance (*svāvidyāpada*) characterized by practice and the mental modification in the form of the indivisible—have reached a state of negation (*apahnava*), Brahman, devoid of the calculation of cause and effect, remains as its own self alone. Then he asks, "What follows from that? and says "Now... (49). Now, after the dispelling of the delusion of cause and effect, that very reality which is beyond the reach of words and established by the awakening to the impossibility of the aggregate of organs—that same reality which appeared in the state of one’s own ignorance as various impure forms, becomes pure by relying on its own nature in the state of self-knowledge. In truth, whether the delusion of the vision of one’s own ignorance exists or not, the pure reality remains as its own self alone. To the question, "If Brahman is one’s own self alone, how is it realized?"—[the answer is: for those whose minds are purified by the performance of good deeds, there subsequently arises the knowledge consisting of the mental modification in the form of the indivisible, born from hearing the Vedānta and so forth. That knowledge, cultivated through intense yoga—that is, through the indivisible, thought-free *samādhi* (*akhaṇḍa-nirvikalpa-samādhi*)—becomes that very reality which is of the nature of certainty. Since this is so, the wise man—having, through the power of perfect knowledge, brought the visible world (which in the state of one’s own ignorance is the collection of the state of one’s own ignorance and its effects) to a state of invisibility, i.e., non-existence—should contemplate it in the form of Brahman. (50) Having thus contemplated the visible world in the form of Brahman with an intellect filled with the essence of consciousness, he should abide in bliss, in the eternally blissful Brahman, as his own remainder. (51) The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the chapter.
Thus ends the first chapter.
The second chapter:
The state of everything being of one indivisible essence.
Then the youth asked Śiva, "Please explain the nature of that which is the indivisible, single-flavored essence of pure consciousness. Paramaśiva replied:
"The visible world is the indivisible, single-flavored essence; the universe is the indivisible, single-flavored essence;
existence itself is the indivisible, single-flavored essence; and you yourself are the indivisible, single-flavored essence. (1)
The mantra is of undivided, single flavor; the ritual action is of undivided, single flavor;
knowledge is of undivided, single flavor; and the water is of undivided, single flavor. (2)
The earth is of undivided, single flavor; the sky is of undivided, single flavor;
the scripture is of undivided, single flavor; and the three Vedas are of undivided, single flavor. (3)
Brahman is the indivisible, single essence, and it is enveloped by the indivisible, single essence;
the individual soul (jīva) is the indivisible, single essence, for the unborn (aja) is indeed the indivisible, single essence.
Brahmā is the indivisible single essence; Hari is the indivisible single essence;
Rudra is the indivisible single essence; I am the indivisible single essence. || 5 ||
For the Self is indeed indivisible and of one essence; the Guru is indivisible and of one essence;
the target of realization is indivisible and of one essence; the Great Splendor is indivisible and of one essence.
The body is the indivisible single essence; the mind is the indivisible single essence;
the consciousness is the indivisible single essence; and bliss is the indivisible single essence.
Knowledge is indivisible and of one essence; the imperishable is indivisible and of one essence;
the eternal is indivisible and of one essence; the supreme is indivisible and of one essence. (8)
There is something that is an unbroken, single essence; it is the supreme unbroken, single essence.
O Six-faced One, there exists nothing other than this unbroken, single essence.
There is nothing other than the partless, single-flavored [reality]; indeed, there is nothing apart from the partless, single-flavored [reality].
From the partless, single-flavored [reality], I am not distinct; I am the partless, single-flavored [reality] itself.
The gross and the subtle are of one indivisible essence, and their form is indivisible;
the object of knowledge is of one indivisible essence, and You are that one indivisible essence.
The secret is the indivisible single essence, beginning with the indivisible single essence;
the knower is the indivisible single essence, and the state is the indivisible single essence. || 12 ||
The mother is of unbroken, singular essence; the father is of unbroken, singular essence;
the brother is of unbroken, singular essence; the husband is of unbroken, singular essence. || 13 ||
The Sūtra is of undivided, single essence; the Virāṭ is of undivided, single essence;
the body is of undivided, single essence; the head is of undivided, single essence.
It is of unbroken, single flavor both internally and externally;
it is the complete, unbroken, single-flavored nectar of immortality. || 15 ||
The lineage is of unbroken, singular essence; the home is of unbroken, singular essence;
the cowherd woman is of unbroken, singular essence; and the moon is of unbroken, singular essence.
The stars are of undivided, single flavor; the sun is of undivided, single flavor;
the sacred field is of undivided, single flavor; and the earth is of undivided, single flavor. (17)
He is the undivided single essence, the peaceful; He is the quality that is the undivided single essence;
He is the witness who is the undivided single essence; He is the friend who is the undivided single essence. || 18 ||
The kinsman is of unbroken, singular essence; the friend is of unbroken, singular essence;
the king is of unbroken, singular essence; the city is of unbroken, singular essence. (19)
The kingdom is of unbroken, singular essence; the subjects are of unbroken, singular essence;
the *tāra* is of unbroken, singular essence; and the recitation (*japa*) is of unbroken, singular essence. (20)
Meditation is of unbroken, singular essence; the state is of unbroken, singular essence;
that which is to be grasped is of unbroken, singular essence; the Great is of unbroken, singular essence.
The light is of undivided, singular essence; the wealth is of undivided, singular essence;
the food is of undivided, singular essence; the oblation is of undivided, singular essence. || 22 ||
The fire-oblation is the indivisible single essence; victory is the indivisible single essence.
Heaven is the indivisible single essence; he himself is the indivisible single essence.

Whatever is seen, whatever is heard, and whatever is remembered within the state of one's own ignorance and its effects—which are imagined by one's own lack of self-knowledge—all that is perceived as being fragmentary and consisting of non-consciousness (acit-mātra). Beyond that, does anything exist that is partless, of a single essence, or pure consciousness (cit-mātra)? Desiring to know the extent of that [reality], Kumāra Skanda—though already knowing it—asked the omniscient Śiva, "Please explain the partless, single-essence pure consciousness," for the sake of favoring the world. To him who had thus questioned him, Paramaśiva spoke; this is introduced with the word "atha" (now). What was it? It is the partless, single-essence visible [reality], and so forth. (1–23)
The contemplation of the pure consciousness-nature of all things:
one should contemplate that everything is the indivisible, single-flavored pure consciousness.
Pure consciousness alone is pure consciousness—the indivisible, single-flavored essence. (24)
(61) Pure consciousness alone, free from becoming, is indeed everything;
for all this is composed of pure consciousness and is indeed nothing but pure consciousness. || 25 ||
They know the individual self (ātmabhāva) to be pure consciousness alone, an undivided single essence;
they know the entire world to be pure consciousness alone, and both "thou-ness" and "I-ness" to consist of pure consciousness.
Space, earth, water, air, fire, Brahmā, Hari, and Śiva—
whatever exists and whatever does not exist— all is indeed pure consciousness alone.
Everything is indeed the undivided, single essence, for it is nothing but pure consciousness;
whatever has been, whatever is, and whatever will be—all that is indeed nothing but pure consciousness. (28)
Substance and time are pure consciousness; knowledge and the object of knowledge are indeed consciousness alone.
The knower is of the nature of pure consciousness, for everything is composed of consciousness alone. (29)
Even conversation is pure consciousness, for whatever is indeed nothing but pure consciousness;
both the non-existent and the existent are pure consciousness, beginningless and endless, eternally composed of consciousness.
The beginning and the end are pure consciousness alone; the teacher, the disciple, and so forth are composed of consciousness.
If the seer and the seen are indeed nothing but pure consciousness, then everything is eternally composed of consciousness.
Everything is the wonder of pure consciousness alone; indeed, the body is nothing but pure consciousness.
Neither the subtle body (liṅga) nor the causal body exists apart from pure consciousness.
Both you and I are pure consciousness alone; the manifest and unmanifest, and all else, consist of consciousness.
Merit and demerit are pure consciousness alone; the individual soul (jīva) has consciousness as its very form. || 33 ||
There is no volition apart from pure consciousness; there is no perception apart from pure consciousness.
There are no mantras and the like apart from pure consciousness; there is no deity apart from pure consciousness.
(62) There is no world-protector apart from pure consciousness; the phenomenal world does not exist apart from pure consciousness.
The supreme Brahman is nothing but pure consciousness; indeed, there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from pure consciousness. 35.
There is no illusion apart from pure consciousness, and there is no worship apart from pure consciousness;
there is nothing to be thought apart from pure consciousness, and there is no reality apart from pure consciousness.
Apart from pure consciousness (cinmātra), there is no sheath (kośa) and so forth; apart from pure consciousness, there is indeed no wealth;
apart from pure consciousness, there is neither silence (mauna) nor non-silence (amaunaka).
There is no detachment apart from pure consciousness alone; for everything is indeed nothing but pure consciousness.
Whatever exists, however much it exists, and whatever is perceived—all that is pure consciousness.
Whatever exists, however much, and however far away—it is indeed all pure consciousness alone;
whatever has come into being, however much, and whatever is perceived—[it is all consciousness]. (39)
Whatever exists and however much there is—all the Vedāntas are indeed nothing but pure consciousness (cinmātra).
There is no going beyond pure consciousness, and there is no liberation apart from pure consciousness.
There is no object of perception other than pure consciousness; indeed, everything is pure consciousness alone.
Brahman is the indivisible, single essence, for nothing exists apart from pure consciousness. (41)
In the scripture, in me, and in you, the Lord, you are indeed of one undivided essence.

There is no doubt whatsoever that Brahman—which is established through the negation (*apahnava*) of the entire mass of effects arising from the state of ignorance (*avidyā*) that is distinct from itself—always remains as non-dual, partless, homogeneous pure Consciousness (*cinmātra*) devoid of any counter-correlate, whether the delusion of one’s own ignorance and other such views exists or not. That very same [Brahman] appears as a reality possessing attributes (*vaidharmya*) superimposed upon Itself in the form of the insentient world of objects (*dṛśya-jagat*) and so forth, according to the perspective of the ignorant. Likewise, this superimposed duality presented by the ignorant appears as merely "empirical" (*vyāvahārika*) to those who possess knowledge born solely from the scriptures; however, to the *vijñānins*, it appears as "illusory" (*prātibhāsika*), and to those of perfect realization...

(p. 63) It is empty; however, to those who know reality, the entire collection of distinctions consisting of the perceived world, existence, and so forth—which are attributed by their own ignorance—shines forth as nothing but non-dual, partless, pure Consciousness alone, which is devoid of any counter-correlate. The collection of distinctions perceived through the vision of one's own ignorance and others belongs only to that vision of one's own ignorance; it cannot possibly touch the Reality, because the Reality is its own non-relational self alone. In this regard, it is seen here also: "Only Being exists; everything else is non-existent. Only Brahman exists; the non-existent does not exist.
Indeed, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of all spiritual scriptures (*adhyātma-śāstra*) is the negation of everything.
"There is no ignorance here, nor is there illusion; this Brahman is peaceful and free from fatigue," and so forth.
To the succession of the ignorant, reality appears as being contrary to the imperishable [Brahman];
however, to the wise, the learned, those with right knowledge, and those who know the ultimate truth, it appears as such in due order.
The object of knowledge (jñeya) may appear as the visible, the false, the empty, or pure consciousness, according to the distinctions [of one's perspective];
such are the various errors of perception, yet they do not belong to the Self (ātman).

This is because of such scriptural passages (*śruti*) and because of the description of the Supreme Imperishable (*paramākṣara*). The established meaning is that nothing exists apart from the undivided, single-flavored pure consciousness (*akhaṇḍaikarasacinmātra*). In the phrase "the undivided, single-flavored state" (*akhaṇḍaikarasaṃ bhāvam*), as well as in phrases like "distinction of time" (*kālabhedam*) which will be mentioned in this chapter and in subsequent chapters, the change in gender (*liṅgavyatyaya*) is a Vedic license (*chāndasa*). The remainder is clear. (24–41)
Or he who knows [it] as "this is the fruit of knowledge" through its uniform nature, or as "I am indeed [that]. || 42 ||
Liberation occurs through knowledge gained once; in the case of perfect knowledge, the teacher is oneself.
Thus [it is said].

He concludes the fruit of knowledge with the word "iti" (thus). From the passage beginning with "The visible world is the undivided single essence" up to the end—"That which exists as the undivided single essence, the Supreme Self, in the scripture, in me, and in you, the Lord—that alone are you, and nothing else"—whoever, by virtue of this uniform nature, knows "I am indeed this very undivided single essence of pure consciousness," he is the one who possesses such knowledge. The locative case here has the sense of the instrumental (*samyagjñānetṛtīyārthe saptamī*); thus, by means of perfect knowledge, he is a Guru, the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman.

Or, having become most excellent, he remains [in that state]. Then, through the knowledge of Brahman alone—which is once-for-all manifest and devoid of any counterpart—there occurs liberation with the physical body (vikalebara-mukti). The word "iti" signifies the conclusion of the chapter. || 42-43 ||
Thus ends the second chapter.
The third chapter:
The experience of the Self as the Brahman of Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
The prince asked his father, "Please describe your own experience. The Blessed One, Paramaśiva, replied:
"I am the nature of the Supreme Brahman; I am supreme bliss.
I am pure consciousness alone; I am the absolute Supreme alone. (1)
I am solely of a peaceful nature; I am solely composed of consciousness;
I am solely of an eternal nature; I am solely everlasting. || 2 ||
I am pure being alone; having abandoned the notion of "I," I am simply "I.
I am of a nature devoid of all else; I consist of the space of consciousness. || 3 ||
I am solely of the nature of the Fourth State (turya), I am the absolute state beyond the Fourth (turyātīta);
I am eternally of the nature of consciousness, and I consist of the bliss of pure awareness (cidānanda). || 4 ||
I am of the nature of absolute form; I am eternally of pure form.
I am solely of the nature of knowledge; I am solely the beloved. || 5 ||
I am of the nature of non-conceptuality; I am effortless and free from affliction.
I am of the nature of eternal non-attachment; I am changeless and immutable.
I am always of the nature of a single essence; I am always whose form is pure consciousness alone.
I am of an unlimited nature, indeed possessing the form of infinite bliss.
I am the nature of supreme bliss; I am the supreme bliss of consciousness. I am the innermost essence within all, beyond the reach of speech and mind.
I am the very nature of self-bliss; I am eternally the bliss of truth. I am the very nature of one who delights in the Self; indeed, I am the Self, Sadāśiva.
I am indeed of the nature of self-luminosity; I am the essence of the light of the Self.
I am devoid of beginning, middle, and end; I am indeed like space.
I am the imperishable one, consisting solely of the existence of eternal, pure consciousness and bliss;
I am the eternally awakened, pure, singular reality of being, consciousness, and bliss.
I am the eternally remaining essential nature; I am forever transcendent of all.
I am the essential nature beyond form, having the supreme ether as my body.
I am the very nature of the bliss of plenitude; I am forever devoid of speech.
I am the form of the substratum of all; I am always a mass of consciousness.
I am devoid of the state of having a body; I am forever free from anxiety;
I am devoid of mental fluctuations; I am the singular essence of the conscious Self.
I am indeed devoid of all that is visible; I alone am the very nature of the Seer. I am always of a complete form, and I am eternally satisfied at all times.
I am indeed Brahman, for everything is I; I am indeed consciousness alone. I am truly I, possessing the essential nature of the form of the Infinite (Bhūman). 16.
I alone am the Great Self; I alone am higher than the highest.
I appear as if I were another, yet I alone exist as if possessing a body.
I indeed appear as a disciple, for I am the refuge of the three worlds;
I transcend the three periods of time, and I am worshipped by the Vedas. || 18 ||
I am determined by the scripture; I am established in the mind. There is nothing whatsoever abandoned by me, nor even the earth itself is abandoned by me. (19)
Whatever else exists apart from Māyā, determine that it does not exist;
"I am Brahman, I am perfected, I am eternally pure forever. (20)
I am devoid of qualities, the absolute Self; I am forever formless.
I am solely the Brahman alone; indeed, I am undecaying and immortal.
I alone shine by myself; I alone am eternally of the nature of existence;
I alone am established in my own self; I alone am the supreme goal.
He himself eats by himself; he himself rejoices by himself;
he himself is self-luminous; he himself is his own glory.
I shall delight in my own self by myself; I shall behold only within my own self.
Seated in bliss within my own self, I shall remain with nothing remaining but my own self alone.
I shall remain established in my own consciousness; I delight in the happiness of the kingdom of my own self.
Seated upon the throne of my own self, I think of nothing other than my own self.
Brahman alone, which is pure consciousness, is existence-consciousness-bliss, non-dual;
I am indeed a mass of bliss, I am the absolute Brahman. (26)
I am always entirely empty; I am the vehicle of the bliss of the Self of all.
I am the nature of eternal bliss; I am always the space of the Self.
I alone, possessing the nature of the sun of consciousness within the space of the heart, am satisfied by myself in the Self; for I am formless and immutable.
I am liberated from the notion of unity, possessing the nature of eternal liberation;
I am subtler than even space, bearing the absence of beginning and end.
I am the form of all illumination; I am the bliss of the supreme and the subordinate. I am whose essential nature is pure existence alone, possessing the very nature of pure liberation.
I am the very nature of truth and bliss; I am a mass of the bliss of knowledge.
I am of the form of pure consciousness alone, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
All this is nothing but Brahman; there is nothing whatsoever other than Brahman. I am that very eternal blissful Brahman; I am indeed the eternal Brahman.
"That which is 'thou' is that which is 'this'; there is nothing whatsoever other than me.
I am the nature of pure consciousness, I alone am the supreme Śiva. (33)
I am of the nature of supreme being; I alone am of the nature of bliss.
Because I am devoid of any object to be witnessed, I never possess the state of being a witness.
Because I am solely the state of Brahman alone, I am the eternal Self;
I alone am the primordial Śeṣa, I am Śeṣa, and indeed, I alone am he.
I am liberated from name and form; I am the embodiment of bliss.
I am of the nature of the absence of sense organs, yet I am the essential nature of all existing things. (36)
I am devoid of bondage and liberation; I am the embodiment of eternal bliss. I am the nature of primordial consciousness; I am the indivisible, single essence. || 37 ||
I am beyond the reach of speech and mind, the vehicle of happiness everywhere;
I am the full form in all places, consisting of the bliss of the Infinite (Bhūmā). || 38 ||
Everywhere I am of the nature of contentment; I am the supreme nectar-essence.
I am indeed the one, non-dual, existent Brahman—of this there is no doubt. (39)
I am the very nature of universal emptiness, the object of all scriptures;
I am liberated, I am the form of liberation, and I possess the nature of the bliss of nirvāṇa.
I am pure consciousness of truth alone; I possess the bliss of pure existence;
I am of a form transcending the fourth state (turiyatita); I possess a nature free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa). || 41 ||
For I am always of an ageless form; I am passionless and stainless. I am pure, I am awakened, I am eternal, and I am the Lord.

"I am the very nature of the meaning of the syllable *Oṃ*; I consist of the stainless. Having thus heard from the mouth of his own father the full extent of the Consciousness that is the one indivisible essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasacinmātra*), the youth asks for his own direct experience therein; thus it is said: "The youth [asks]. Accepting that question, [the father says]: "I am of the nature of that Supreme Brahman, which is the experience of the one indivisible essence of pure consciousness—transcending and distinct from everything imagined by those ignorant of themselves—and which perfectly nourishes and unfolds [all things]. [The word] 'paramānandam' [is used with] a change of gender [from masculine to neuter]."

(69) "I am supreme bliss"—this is the meaning. Furthermore: "Kevalam" (alone), etc. Because it is inwardly luminous, it is of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*); because it is the most excellent of all, it is *parama* (supreme). || 1 || Because there is no cruel thing other than itself, it is *śānta* (peaceful); because the impermanent has perished, it is *nitya* (eternal); because it is without end, it is *śāśvata* (everlasting). || 2 || Because it is the Lord (*īśvara*), it is of the nature of pure being (*sattva*). Having abandoned the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) that is inward-looking yet dependent on the external, I am the remaining ego-sense. In the realization "All is Brahman," I am the Brahman alone established by the negation of everything else. Consisting of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), I am the very essence of the space of consciousness. || 3 || It is the Fourth (*turya*), the inward-facing; beyond that is the Transcendent (*para*). Because of the absence of all distinctions, it is *kevala* (absolute). || 4–5 || Because it cannot be grasped by conceptual thought, it is *nirvikalpa* (free from conceptualization); because of the absence of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it is *nirīha* (inactive); because of the destruction of the disease of worldly existence, it is *nirāmaya* (free from affliction); even while adjuncts (*upādhi*) exist, it is unattached (*asaṅga*); because of the absence of modification, it is *nirvikāra* (unchanging); because of the absence of decay through self or another, it is *avyaya* (undecaying). || 6 || It is unlimited (*aparicchinna*) due to the absence of the three kinds of limitation. It is infinite bliss (*anantānanda*) because its nature is immeasurable bliss. || 7 || It is of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Supreme Bliss (*saccitparānanda*) because its nature is Being-Consciousness-Supreme Bliss. It is within all; more internal than that is the Transcendent, because it is the nature of Brahman non-different from the inward-facing Self. It is beyond the range of the collection of organs such as speech and mind. || 8 || Its nature is Truth, Self, and Bliss. It delights in all selves in the form of the inward-facing Self, etc., thus it is *ātmārāma* (delighting in the Self). || 9 || Because it lacks birth, maintenance, and dissolution, it is devoid of beginning, middle, and end. Because it is partless, it is like space (*ākāśa*). || 10 || Because it is the universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*), it is pure existence (*sattāmātra*). || 11 || Because it is the nature of the remainder of all, it is the eternal remainder (*nityaśeṣa*). || 12 || Because its bliss is unlimited, it is the bliss of the Infinite (*bhūmānanda*). Because of the absence of organs such as speech, it is devoid of speech (*bhāṣāhīna*). || 13–14 || Due to the impossibility of an object of sight, it is pure vision (*dṛṅmātra*). || 15–16 || From the perspective of one who does not know themselves, I appear as if I were another, as if teacher and disciple. I am the one to be worshipped and determined by the Vedas and Shastras. || 17–18 || The rest is clear. He says, "That which is left over by me" (*mattyaktam*), meaning: know that there is nothing not pervaded by me, nor anything separate from me. || 19 || Furthermore: "Aham" (I). || 20 || I am absolute Brahman alone, because I am without a counter-correlative (*niṣpratiyogika*). || 21 || Since this entire universe is myself, I do not think of anything other than myself—thus he says, "Svayameva" (myself alone). || 22 || In the word "bhuṅkte" (he eats), there is a change of person; the meaning is "I eat" (*bhuñje*). || 23–25 || He says, "Cit" (Consciousness): that which is merely the form of Consciousness, that alone I am. || 26 || I am always empty of everything, because of the non-existence of everything at all times. || 27 ||

(70) I alone possess the nature of the sun of consciousness (*cidāditya*), because I am the solar consciousness that illumines the thousands of mental fluctuations such as desire residing in the hearts of all living beings. || 28 || I am free from the number "one," because I am incalculable. I am devoid of beginning and end, because there is no origination or dissolution for me. || 29 || I possess the supreme and lower bliss, because I am the bliss of Brahman non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*). I possess the nature of pure liberation, because the liberation from the delusion of anything other than myself is established in my own being. || 30–31 || Since nothing else exists, he says "that alone am I" with the words "Brahman alone" (*brahmamātram*). || 32 || He says "you" (*tvam*) to show that there is nothing separate from me that can be denoted by words such as "you" or "that" (*tad*). || 33 || I am the nature beyond all states of being (*atibhāva*), because I transcend all objective existents. Regarding "witness-ship" (*sākṣitva*): since witness-ship depends upon an object to be witnessed and thus possesses distinctions, the meaning is that I am devoid of that. || 34 || I am the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) like the serpent Śeṣa, because I support the earth (the world). "I am the remainder" (*ahaṃśeṣa*) means that only my own self remains. || 35–38 || I am one only, without a second, because I am devoid of internal, external, and similar differences. || 39 || I am the scope of all the scriptures, because I am known through the Vedānta. I am liberated from the duality of my own ignorance. I possess the form of the bliss of extinction (*nirvāṇa*), because I am the bliss of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*). || 40–41 || I am enlightened (*buddha*), because my nature is pure awakening. || 42 || I am the essential nature of the meaning of the syllable *Oṃ*, because I am the state beyond the fourth (*turyaturya*). || 42 ||
In the Self, there is the experience of the absence of all differentiated forms; I am of the nature of the form of consciousness—neither am I "this," nor am I "that. (43)
For I am not of any specific nature, but possess a nature free from activity;
I am partless and without appearance, neither mind nor am I the senses.
I am neither intellect nor conceptualization; I am not the triad beginning with the body.
I am not of the nature of waking or dreaming, nor do I possess the form of deep sleep.
I am not of the nature of the threefold suffering, nor do I possess the threefold desires;
there is no need for my hearing of the scriptures regarding perfection, nor for reflection upon the conscious Self.
I have nothing of the same class, nor anything of a different class anywhere;
I have nothing pertaining to myself, and nowhere do I possess these threefold distinctions.

(71) That which is denoted by the word "I" (ahaṃśabda) extends from the gross body up to the innermost Self; that which is denoted by the word "That" (tacchabda) extends from Virāṭ up to Turya. Because [the True Self] is distinct from both of these, [it is said]: "I am not this, nor is this I. (43) It has no nature whatsoever apart from itself. Because its meaning is indivisible (akhaṇḍārtha), it is partless (niraṃśa). Because it is distinct from the three bodies, it is not the mind, and so forth. (44–45) Since the Self is established by its own nature, there is no requirement for means such as hearing (śravaṇa); thus he says: "Hearing," etc. The word "and" (ca) serves to include meditative reflection (nididhyāsana). (46) He states that there is no triad of distinctions, such as those of the same class (sajātīya) and so on: "The homogeneous," etc. (47)

The experience of everything other than oneself is unreal; for the form of the mind is unreal, the form of the intellect is unreal, and the ego is unreal. [Yet] I am indeed eternal, everlasting, and unborn.
Know the three bodies to be unreal, and know the three times to be eternally unreal;
know the three qualities (guṇas) to be unreal, for I am the pure Self, whose nature is truth.
Know that all that is heard is always unreal; know that the entire Veda is always unreal;
know indeed that every scripture is unreal, for I am the Reality, whose nature is consciousness.
Know the three forms to be non-existent, and all beings to be eternally non-existent;
know the principle of sattva to be non-existent, for I am the Infinite, Sadāśiva.
Know that the teacher and the disciple are unreal; therefore, know the mantra of the teacher to be unreal as well. Know that whatever is visible is unreal; do not know me to be of such a nature.
Know that which is inconceivable to be non-existent; know that which is logical to always be non-existent;
know that which is beneficial to be non-existent; do not know me to be of such a nature.
Know all living beings to be unreal; know all enjoyments to be unreal.
Know what is seen and heard to be unreal; know that which is woven across and lengthwise to be composed of unreality.
Know that what is to be done and what is not to be done is unreal, destroyed, and composed of unreality;
know that suffering and non-suffering are unreal, and everything and nothingness are composed of unreality. (55)
Know that fullness and emptiness are unreal, and know that dharma and adharma consist of unreality;
know that gain and loss are unreal, and know that victory and defeat consist of unreality.
Know all sound to be unreal; know all touch to be always unreal.
Know all form to be unreal; know all taste to consist of unreality. (57)
Know all fragrance to be non-existent; know all ignorance to consist of the unreal.
Everything is always non-existent; even that which arises from existence is indeed non-existent.
Indeed, all qualities are non-existent; I alone am pure Being (sanmātra).

That which is other than myself, being a mere generality, is absolutely non-existent, like the horn of a hare, existing only in the form of absolute negation. But I am the nature of the state of Brahman alone—non-dual and devoid of any counter-correlate—which is established through the negation of that [generality]; thus he says: "For that which is unreal... (48–58).
One should constantly perceive the mantra of one's own Self and constantly practice the mantra of one's own Self, namely the mantra "I am Brahman. || 59 ||
This mantra "I am Brahman" destroys the evil of the visible world;
this mantra "I am Brahman" destroys all other mantras. (60)
This mantra "I am Brahman" shall destroy the defects of the body;
this mantra "I am Brahman" shall destroy the sins of birth. (61)
This mantra, "I am Brahman," shall destroy the noose of death;
this mantra, "I am Brahman," shall destroy the suffering of duality.
This mantra, "I am Brahman," shall destroy the notion of duality;
this mantra, "I am Brahman," shall destroy the suffering of anxiety. (63)
This mantra "I am Brahman" shall destroy the disease of the intellect;
this mantra "I am Brahman" shall destroy the bondage of the mind. (64)
This mantra, "I am Brahman," shall destroy all diseases;
this mantra, "I am Brahman," shall destroy all sorrow. || 65 ||
This mantra, "I am Brahman," destroys the sequence of [mental] stages and so forth in an instant;
this mantra, "I am Brahman," destroys the state of anger.
This mantra, "I am Brahman," shall destroy the fluctuations of the mind;
this mantra, "I am Brahman," shall destroy volitions and the like. (67)
This mantra, "I am Brahman" (ahaṃ brahmāsmi), shall destroy ten million faults;
this mantra, "I am Brahman," shall destroy all [obstacles] within the Tantras. || 68 ||
This mantra "I am Brahman" shall destroy the ignorance of the Self;
this mantra "I am Brahman" bestows victory over the world of the Self. (69)
This mantra "I am Brahman" bestows inconceivable bliss;
this mantra "I am Brahman" grants non-inertness.
This mantra "I am Brahman" (Ahaṃ Brahmāsmi) is the crusher of the demons of the non-Self;
this thunderbolt of "I am Brahman" shall carry away the mountains known as the non-Self.
"I am Brahman"—this wheel, by virtue of its non-self-nature, shall strike down the demons;
"I am Brahman"—this mantra shall liberate them all. (72)
This mantra, "I am Brahman" (ahaṃ brahmāsmi), bestows knowledge and bliss;
it is a great mantra of seventy million syllables that grants the fruit of hundreds of millions of births. (73)
Having set aside all other mantras, one should practice this mantra;
one attains immediate liberation—of this there is not even the slightest doubt. (74)
Thus [it is said].

Because the practice of the mantra of one’s own Self leads to the attainment of the state of Brahman alone, which is devoid of all counter-correlates, by means of dispelling the obstacles to the realization of Brahman—for this reason, one who desires liberation from the delusion of bondage and release should always practice this very mantra, "I am Brahman. Thus he says: "The mantra of one's own Self" (*svātmamantram*). This meaning is clear. (Verses 59–74). The word *iti* signifies the conclusion of the chapter.
Thus ends the third chapter. || 3 ||
The Fourth Chapter:
Liberation while Living (Jīvanmukti)—the Attainment of the State of Brahman Non-different from the Inner Self.
Kumāra asked the Supreme Lord, "Please describe the state of one liberated while living and one liberated after death. He, the Supreme Śiva, replied:
"I am the conscious self, I am the supreme self, I am devoid of qualities, I am higher than the highest.
He who remains established in the Self alone is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 1 ||
"I am distinct from the three bodies; I am pure consciousness.
He who has the realization 'I am Brahman' within himself is called one liberated while living. (2)
I am of the nature of a mass of bliss; I am a solid mass of supreme bliss.
He for whom there is no body or the like, he who possesses the certainty that "I am Brahman," and he who is filled with supreme bliss—he is called one liberated while living. (3)
He who possesses nothing whatsoever remains as pure consciousness alone;
he whose interior is pure consciousness and whose very nature consists solely of pure consciousness.
His essential nature is complete everywhere; he is the Self that remains as everything.
Manifested in the delight of bliss, he is the perfectly full one whose very being is consciousness.
The Self is of the nature of pure consciousness, entirely free from all attachments;
it is eternal bliss, serene in nature, and indeed devoid of any other thoughts.
He who is devoid of even the slightest sense of existence is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta):
"I have no mind, no intellect, no ego, and no senses. (7)
Never is there a body for me, nor ever are there vital breaths and so forth;
there is no illusion for me, no desire for me, and no anger for me—I am the Supreme.
Neither this nor anything else belongs to me; nowhere in the world does anything belong to me.
I have no fault, no gender-mark, no eye, and no mind.
I have no ear, no nose, no tongue, and no hand;
I have neither waking nor sleep, nor even the slightest cause for them.
He who thinks, "The fourth state does not belong to me," is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
"All this is nothing to me; this whole world belongs to me nowhere at all. (11)
(76) I have no time, no place, no object, and no thought;
I have no ritual bathing, no twilight worship, no deity, and no sacred ground. || 12 ||
I have no sacred ford, no ritual service, no knowledge, and no station; I have no bondage, no birth, no speech, and no sun.
"Neither merit nor sin is mine; neither duty nor auspiciousness is mine;
neither the individual soul nor anything else whatsoever born within the three worlds is mine—such is my own Self. (14)
For me there is no liberation, no duality, no Veda, and no injunction;
for me there is nothing near, nothing far, no awakening, and no secrecy.
I have no teacher, nor do I have a disciple; I have none inferior to me, nor anyone superior.
I am not Brahmā, I am not Viṣṇu, I am not Rudra, nor am I the Moon.
The earth is not mine, nor water is mine, nor wind is mine, nor space is mine; fire is not mine, nor my lineage is mine, nor my object of perception is mine, nor worldly existence is mine. (17)
I have no meditator, no object of meditation, no meditation, and no mantra;
I have neither cold nor heat, neither thirst nor hunger.
I have no friend, no enemy; I have neither delusion nor victory.
I am not before, nor am I behind; I am not above, nor am I the directions.
I have nothing to say, whether it be little; I have nothing to hear, even the slightest; I have nothing to reflect upon, however small; I have nothing to meditate upon, even the most minute.
I have nothing to eat, nor is there even the slightest thing for me to remember;
I have no enjoyment, no passion, no sacrifice, and no dissolution.
(77) I have no foolishness, no peace, no bondage, and no pleasure;
I have neither joy nor rapture, and I am neither corpulent nor emaciated. (22)
For me there is neither long nor short, neither increase nor decrease;
for me there is neither superimposition nor denial, neither unity nor multiplicity.
I have no blindness, nor do I have dullness; not even the slightest stiffness is mine.
I have no flesh, no blood, no fat, and indeed no vital fluid.
I have no marrow, nor my bones, nor my skin—the seven constituent elements; I have no semen, nor my blood, nor my blue, nor am I separate from them. (25)
I have no heat, nor do I have greed; for me there is neither primary nor secondary anywhere.
I have no delusion, nor stability; I have no secret, nor lineage. (26)
Nothing is to be abandoned by me, nothing is to be grasped by me; there is no laughter for me, nor any policy; there is no vow for me, no exhaustion, no withering away, and no pleasure for me.
I have no knower, I have no knowledge, I have no object of knowledge, and I am not myself.
I am not yours, I am not mine, you are not mine, and "I" am not mine. (28)
I have no old age, I have no childhood, and not even the slightest youth belongs to me; "I am Brahman, I am Brahman, I am Brahman"—this is my firm conviction.
Thinking "I am consciousness, I am consciousness," he is called one liberated while living;
"I am indeed Brahman, I am indeed consciousness, I am the Supreme—of this there is no doubt. (30)
The Swan is himself by himself; he is himself established by himself.
He should see himself by himself alone and dwell in the happiness of his own sovereign self-realm. 31.
(78) He who shall himself enjoy the bliss of his own self is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
He alone is remembered as the solitary hero at the forefront; he alone is known as the Lord.
He who shall sleep within his own true nature is called liberated while living. || 32 ||

The Kumāra, having correctly understood from his father Parameśvara primarily the knowledge of the indivisible, single-flavored pure consciousness (*akhaṇḍaikarasacinmātra*) and its direct experience, asks Śiva in order to understand the nature of *jīvanmukti* and *videhamukti*, which constitute the primary intermediate fruits [of that realization]. Thus he says: "The Kumāra... Having accepted that, He (Śiva) spoke in sequence regarding the characteristics of *jīvanmukti* and *videhamukti*. Among these, the characteristic of *jīvanmukti* is stated as: "The conscious Self... The collective meaning of the synonyms for *jīvanmukti* to be mentioned hereafter is: the state of abiding in the inward-facing reality (*pratyagbhāva*) by swallowing up the outward-facing state (*parāgbhāva*), or the attainment of the state of Brahman non-different from the inward-facing reality. || 1–4 || "One whose delight is in the Self of Bliss" (*ānandarati*) refers to one who finds pleasure in the Self alone. || 5 || "Devoid of other thoughts" (*anyacintāvivarjita*) means because everything other than himself is something to be sought after [as an object]. || 6–9 || He describes the distinction from the four states (*avasthācatuṣṭaya*), just as there is a distinction from the three bodies (*dehatraya*): "For me there is no waking... || 10–14 || "For me there is neither injunction nor prohibition"—this is the meaning. || 15–31 || "He is himself the Lord" (*svayameva prabhuḥ*) because of his sovereignty. By this much of the text—starting with "I am the conscious Self" (*cidātmāhaṃ*) and "I am the supreme Self" (*parātmāhaṃ*)"—the characteristics of the *jīvanmukta* divided into the four classes beginning with the "knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*) have been declared. Generally, this *Tejobindu Upaniṣad* has been explained here through incidental discussion (*prasaktānuprasaktyā*) in the light of the "Jewel Garland of Great Sayings" (*Mahāvākyaratnāvalī*) ranging from the injunctions to *videhamukti*; therefore, it is not explained word-by-word again here for fear of excessive prolixity. || 32 ||
Liberation while disembodied (videhamukti) is the state of abiding as one's own self alone, which is Brahman alone, free from all correlates.
Having become Brahman, with a tranquil self, consisting of the bliss of Brahman, and happy;
being of a pure nature and a great silent sage—he is indeed liberated while in the body (vaidehī mukti). || 33 ||
I have arisen as the self of all, the self of equal form, and the pure self;
devoid of duality, the singular self, the self of all, consisting solely of my own self. || 34 ||
I am the unborn self, I am the immortal self; I am the self that is inherently undecaying.
I am the self that is the goal, I am the self that is graceful; I am the one whose nature is the silent self. (35)
The Self is blissful, for the Self is dear; the Self is liberation, free from bondage.
"I am indeed Brahman, I am indeed Consciousness"—even this is not to be contemplated. (36)
He who remains as pure consciousness alone is indeed liberated from the body. || 37 ||
Having abandoned all other certainties and established the certainty that "I am Brahman," he whose heart is filled with bliss—that Vaidehī is indeed liberated. (38)
Having abandoned the certainty that "everything exists" or "it does not exist," he remains as pure Being-Consciousness-Bliss, [realizing] "I am Brahman" and yet "I am not [the ego]. (39)
It does not touch itself anywhere, at any time, or in any way.
Thus it remains in silence; in silence, in silence, there is no truth whatsoever.
The Supreme Self transcends the qualities (guṇas), is the self of all, and the creator of all beings;
He [removes] the distinction of time, the distinction of objects, the distinction of space, and the distinction of Himself.
There is not the slightest difference in him, nor does anything whatsoever exist apart from him; "I," "you," "that," "this," "he," and "this"—he is the self of time, yet devoid of time.
He is the self that is empty, the self whose nature is subtle form, the self of the universe, and that which is devoid of the universe;
the self of the gods, the self devoid of gods, the self that is the object of measurement, and that which is free from objects of measurement. || 43 ||
Everywhere I am the Self devoid of insentience, the innermost Self of all, and the Self devoid of all mental constructs; I am always pure consciousness alone. 44.
I am the absolute Supreme Self alone, the absolute embodiment of knowledge; my nature is that of pure existence, and there is no other world of fear. (45)
"Where is the statement 'the individual soul and the Lord'? "In the Vedas and scriptures. "And where is 'I am this'?
"In the thought 'this is indeed consciousness' and also 'I am consciousness'. (46)
Thus, he who is free from the certainty [of dualistic thought] regarding Vaidehī is indeed liberated;
established in his own self through pure consciousness alone, he finds delight in his own soul and remains seated in bliss.
He whose nature is undivided, who is free from the categories of atomic and gross,
who is the fourth of the fourth (turyātīta), the supreme bliss— he is indeed liberated as Vaidehī.
The Self is devoid of name and form, consisting of the bliss of supreme consciousness;
its nature transcends the fourth state (turīya), and it is free from both the auspicious and the inauspicious. || 49 ||
The self of yoga, whose self is united with yoga, is devoid of both bondage and liberation;
its self is free from qualities and the absence of qualities, and it is devoid of space, time, and so forth. || 50 ||
Devoid of the nature of both witness and witnessed, it is neither something nor nothing;
for it, even the manifestation of the phenomenal world here does not possess the form of Brahman.
Self-luminous in its own nature, finding its own delight in its own nature;
bliss beyond the reach of words, it is itself beyond the range of speech and mind.
O Vaidehī, that which is the state beyond the past is indeed liberated;
it is that which transcends the fluctuations of the mind and is the illuminator of those mental fluctuations.
With his self devoid of all mental fluctuations, that Videha is indeed liberated;
at that time, he is called "Videha" because he is free from the recollection of the body.
If one remembers even for a mere moment that which is traditionally taught, then one becomes endowed with everything:
the inner self unseen by others, a dense mass of supreme bliss and consciousness. (55)
Its external nature unseen by others, it is the domain of all Vedānta;
it is the savoring of the nectar-essence of Brahman, the elixir of the nectar-essence of Brahman.
Attached to the nectar-essence of Brahman, he is himself the nectar-essence of Brahman;
immersed in the nectar-essence of Brahman, he performs the worship of the auspicious Bliss of Brahman.
Satiated by the nectar-essence of Brahman, he is the experiencer of the bliss of Brahman;
he is the bliss of Brahman and the bliss of Śiva, radiant with the essence of the bliss of Brahman.
The supreme light of the bliss of Brahman, uninterrupted by the bliss of Brahman;
one who eats the food of the essence of the bliss of Brahman, whose family is the bliss of Brahman. || 59 ||
