Mounted upon the essence of the bliss of Brahman, a single mass of consciousness consisting solely of the bliss of Brahman, he is wedded to the bliss of Brahman and is a treasury of the bliss of Brahman. || 60 ||
Endowed with those who have attained the bliss of Brahman, he abides in the Self that is the bliss of Brahman;
all this is the form of the Self, and there is nothing whatsoever other than the Self.
Everything is the Self; I am the Self; I am the Supreme Self, whose nature is the Highest Self.
The Self is of the nature of eternal bliss; he who realizes this is indeed liberated as Vaidehī.
The Great Self is of perfect form, the joyful self, and of eternal nature;
He is the self whose form is the inner ruler of all, the stainless self, and the selfless one.
The Self whose nature is changeless is the pure Self, whose form is peace;
its essential nature is both peaceful and non-peaceful, yet it is devoid of any state of manifoldness.

(82) Devoid of the entire conceptualization of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman), its nature is both liberated and unliberated, yet it is free from the distinction between liberation and bondage. || 65 ||
The Self whose nature consists of bondage and liberation is devoid of bondage and liberation;
the Self whose nature consists of duality and non-duality is devoid of duality and non-duality. || 66 ||
His self is the nature of both the all and the not-all, yet he is devoid of both the all and the not-all;
his self is the nature of joy and intense joy, yet he is entirely free from joy and the like.
Devoid of all conceptual constructions, that Vaidehī is indeed liberated;
she is the partless self, the stainless self, the awakened self, and the essential self of the Puruṣa.
The Self devoid of bliss and so forth, the immortal Self whose nature is immortality;
the Self whose nature is the three times, yet free from the three times. (69)
For he is the soul of all, the immeasurable self, the self of all measures, yet devoid of measurement;
his nature is eternally perceptible, and he is determined by eternal perception.

The Self whose nature is not diminished by anything else, who is self-luminous and not dependent on others; whose essence consists of the objects of knowledge such as wisdom and ignorance, yet who is himself devoid of wisdom, ignorance, and the like. (71)
The self is devoid of permanence and impermanence, free from this world and the next;
it is a self devoid of the six qualities beginning with tranquility, and free from the desire for liberation and so forth. || 72 ||
The Self is devoid of the gross body, free from the subtle body,
devoid of the causal body and so forth, and free even from the fourth state (turīya) and beyond.
The Self is devoid of the sheath of food, bereft of the sheath of vital breath;
the Self is devoid of the sheath of mind, and free from consciousness and the rest. || 74 ||
The Self is devoid of the sheath of bliss and is free from the five sheaths;
it is the Self whose nature is beyond conceptual construction and is entirely free from conceptualization. || 75 ||
Pervaded by the visible yet devoid of a low self, pierced by sound yet free from it;
always characterized by a void-self in meditative absorption, and devoid of beginning, middle, and end. (76)

One whose self is devoid of wisdom and speech, who is bereft of the realization "I am Brahman," whose self is lacking the [teachings] such as "That thou art," and who does not perceive "this is the Self"—[is such a person]. (77)
The self denoted by the syllable *oṃ* is devoid of [all] that is denotable; it is free from everything that can be expressed.
Its nature is devoid of the three states; it is the imperishable self, consisting of pure consciousness. || 78 ||

Devoid of a self that is to be known and so forth, whose nature consists of whatever this [world] may be, and whose self is free from appearance and disappearance—that one belonging to Videha is indeed liberated. (79)

Brahman, established through the negation of the entire conceptualization consisting of the state of ignorance and its effects—which are other than oneself—is non-dual, being one's own self alone. Abiding in that alone is the definition of disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*). This is now elaborated upon with the verse beginning "He who has become Brahman" (*brahmabhūta*). "Become Brahman" (*brahmabhūta*) means because he abides as nothing but Brahman. "With a tranquil self" (*praśāntātmā*) means because the identification with the three bodies has been stilled. "Consisting of the bliss of Brahman" (*brahmānandamaya*) means his nature is bliss; the meaning is that he is solely the peerless bliss of the Infinite (*bhūmā*). "Of transparent form" (*svaccharūpa*) means because his nature is perfect consciousness (*pūrṇabodha*). "The great silent sage" (*mahāmaunī*) means because he remains in silence as his own self alone. Regarding the term "disembodied" (*videha*): the state of ignorance and the collection of its effects, characterized by the three bodies, are called "bodies" (*deha*) because they are rooted in the identification of "self" and "mine. Those [identifications] have departed, and thus they are "disembodied" (*videha*). Those very disembodied states are "the disembodied" (*vaideha*), and he possesses them, hence he is "one of the disembodied" (*vaidehī*). Lest it be thought that one designated by such a state might still be bound, the text says "liberated" (*mukta*). Where everything other than himself is liberated—that is, has reached the state of negation—he is indeed "one of the disembodied liberated ones" (*vaidehī mukta*). This is the point.

He in whom the latent impressions of the gross body and so forth— known as the individual and the collective— undergo a transformation into their opposite, is the great sage who is "bodiless" (videha).
For he alone is established as Brahman alone through the negation of everything;
indeed, it is sung everywhere that this is the most excellent state, free from all conceptual construction.

Thus, the *Smṛti* is the authority. In this very same way, the scriptural texts concerning liberation while in the body (*videhamukti*) are to be understood. (33) Furthermore—“The Self of all” (*sarvātmā*): He consists solely of His own Self, because He is of a single nature devoid of any counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika*). (34) “The Self that is the goal” (*lakṣyātmā*): Because He is defined by the fact that nothing remains but Himself. “The Graceful Self” (*lalitātmā*): Because He is exclusively non-differentiated (*kevalanirviśeṣa*). “The Self whose nature is silence” (*tūṣṇīmātmasvabhāvavān*): Because He is the very form of the fruit of great silence (*mahāmauna*). (35) He is not thought of, because even such a thought, being a modification of consciousness (*vidyāvṛtti*), must be negated. (36) By the word "and" (*ca*), [the text implies] the certainty that "there is something other than Himself" and "there is nothing [other than Himself]. (37–39) Where the multitude of those ignorant of their own Self transmigrates, there the man of knowledge (*jñānī*) or the man of realized wisdom (*vijñānī*), through detachment from worldly attachment, becomes subject to the undivided mental state (*akhaṇḍākāravṛtti*) whose object is Brahman non-different from the Inner Self (*pratyagabhinnabrahmagocara*), and thus remains silent in this manner. If, however, a yogi or a man of perfect knowledge cannot endure even this undivided mental state, he becomes subject to the thought-free absorption (*nirvikalpakasamādhi*) and remains silent for some time. Regarding the statement "Silence is Truth; there is nothing whatsoever": the knower of Reality, unable to endure even occasional emergence from the thought-free absorption established by the dissolution of forms (*sarūpavilaya*), remains in His silent nature as the mere non-dual Brahman devoid of counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogikanirvikalpa*), having accomplished the negation of the entire collection of conceptualizations consisting of His own ignorance, duality, and their effects—both internal and external—within the radiant space of Consciousness (*cidākāśa*) shining in the *kaivalyanāḍī* within the *suṣumnā* channel. That which remains as the mere Being (*sanmātra*), characterized by the state of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*), is the Truth. Therein, there is no delusion that "something other than Himself exists" or "does not exist," because of such scriptural passages as: "There is nothing other than Brahman"; "Not even an atom exists apart from Me"; and "Being alone is real, the rest is unreal. (40–41) Where one would say "difference" (*bheda*), the change of case is made to "difference" (*bhedam*). (42–45) Where one would say "Jīva and Īśvara," the vocative is used as "O Jīva and Īśvara" (*jīveśvara*); where one would say "Vedas and Śāstras," the change of gender is made to "O Vedas and Śāstras" (*vedaśāstra*). (46–47) "The Fourth of the Fourth" (*turyaturya*): Because its nature is the non-conceptualization of non-conceptualization. (48–49)

(85) The Self is devoid of qualities and defects, for even that which is "without qualities" (nirguṇa) is characterized by distinctions when it is dependent upon the three qualities (triguṇa). The meaning is that this Self is the "qualityless" (nirguṇa) one who is free from the opposition between the relative states of being "with qualities" and "without qualities," which are mutually dependent. || 50 || The entire range of things defined as objects of perception (sākṣya) and the perceiver (sākṣin), whether they appear as something or not, is actually nothing at all. || 51–60 || Whatever was tasted before liberation while in the body—such as food and the like—and whatever was performed, such as maintaining a family through marriage and so forth, or the worship of Śiva—all that now becomes nothing but the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*). This is because for one liberated while in the body (*videhamukta*), there is the established negation of any mental construction (*kalanā*) other than oneself, as well as the activity and cessation of such constructions. He says, "It is the nature of the Self" (verse 61–62), to show that nothing exists apart from the state of liberation while in the body. || 61–62 || It is "without self" (*nirātmaka*) because it is the pure consciousness of the Lord’s witness (*īśvara-sākṣicid-mātra*). || 63–66 || It is "devoid of all and everything" because the dualities of bondage and liberation, duality and non-duality, and so forth, are characterized by distinctions based on mutual dependence; the meaning is that this Self is the non-dual reality (*advaitātman*) which has no counterpart. || 67–69 || It is "determined by constant direct perception"; the meaning is that it is determined by those ignorant of themselves and others, each according to their own particular perspective. || 70–73 || Since it might be thought that the four Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) possess both the expressed (*vācya*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*) meanings, he says, "The net of wisdom" (*prajñāna*) and so forth. || 77–81 ||
The rule for abiding in one's own self:
Behold only the Self; awaken your own Self;
enjoy your own Self by yourself; remain established in your own well-being, O Six-faced One. (80)
Satisfied with yourself by yourself within your own self, move about as your own self;
rejoice in the self alone, and become liberated, O Vaidehī.
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
Thus, the word "Upaniṣad" signifies the conclusion of the narrative concerning Kumāraśiva. || 82 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter. || 4 ||
The Fifth Chapter: The True Nature of One's Own Self.
A sage named Nidāgha questioned the venerable Ṛbhu, saying, "Please explain the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self. The venerable Ṛbhu replied:
Brahman is the limit of all speech, the Guru is the limit of all thought;
He is the self of all causes and effects, yet devoid of cause and effect. || 1 ||
Śiva is free from all mental constructs, consists entirely of resonance (nāda), is pure consciousness devoid of everything else, and is the supreme one composed of universal bliss. || 2 ||
Its essence is the radiance of all splendor, consisting of the bliss of *nāda*;
it is free from all experience and devoid of all meditation. || 3 ||
This immutable Self, which is I, transcends all sounds and parts;
it is devoid of distinctions such as the discrimination between self and non-self, or between difference and non-difference.
The Self is devoid of such qualities as peace and non-peace; it is the form of light within the inner sound (nāda).
It is far removed from the meaning of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), and the realization "I am Brahman" is even further removed from it.
That which is devoid of the word "that" (tat), free from the word "thou" (tvam), devoid of the meaning of a sentence,
and free from both the perishable and the imperishable— that is indeed the light within the resonance (nāda).
I am indeed the undivided, single essence, the bliss free from all [limitations];
my self-nature transcends everything, and I am the light within the sound (nāda). || 7 ||
That which is devoid of the word "self," that which is free from the referent of the word "self," and that which is devoid of existence, consciousness, and bliss—this alone is the eternal Self. (8)
He is impossible to describe, being inaccessible even through the sentences of the Vedas;
of whom there is nothing outside, nothing inside, and not even anything of a limited measure.
For whom the *liṅga* or the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is indeed Brahman itself as the Self— of this there is no doubt—
for him there exists neither a body nor a living soul (*jīva*) composed of the elements and their derivatives.
For him there exists no name-and-form and so forth, neither the object of enjoyment nor the enjoyer;
he has neither existence nor non-existence, nor even a state of being either perishable or imperishable.

Whether possessing qualities or devoid of them, he is my Self; of this there is no doubt—for him there is neither the expressed nor the expresser, neither that which is heard nor the act of reflection.
Neither the distinction between teacher and disciple, nor the worlds of the gods, nor the gods and asuras,
perceive therein even the slightest atom of dharma or adharma, or of purity or impurity.
Where there is no certainty or doubt regarding whether it is the right time or the wrong time; where there exists neither mantra nor non-mantra, neither knowledge nor ignorance.
Or rather, the seer, the seeing, and the seen are merely a slight portion consisting of limited power (kalā).

Along with Kumāra was one named Ṛbhu, the mental son of Brahmā; he too, having understood from the mouth of Śiva the full extent of both *jīvanmukti*—which consists of the knowledge of pure consciousness as an unbroken single essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasa-cinmātra*), its experience, and the primary fruit existing in the interval between them—and *videhamukti*, truly attained the state of having accomplished all that was to be done. Once, a sage named Nidāgha, having heard it stated in all the Vedas, Śāstras, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth, that "the Self and the non-Self exist," asked him out of a desire to know their full extent; thus says the Śruti: "Nidāgha. Having accepted his question, [he spoke].

He said: "What is that? To this, [the answer is] "The end of all speech. It is the limit of all speech because it is beyond sound (*aśabda*). It is the limit of all thought, because the Self (*pratīc*) swallows up the functions of thought and the like. From the perspective of one's own ignorance (*svājña*), it is the essence of all causes and effects. (1) It consists of all sound (*sarvanādamaya*), because it is the meaning of the established conclusions of the Vedas and scriptures as expressed through sound and its derivatives. It is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) devoid of everything attributed by the ignorant. (2) Since there might be the notion of having attributes (*saviśeṣatā*) regarding that which is the object of one's own experience, meditation, and so forth, he says: "The end of all... (3–4). Since the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*)—the identity of *tat* and *tvam*—is the Self, he says: "By the great sentence... (5). It is devoid of the perishable and the imperishable (*kṣarākṣara-vihīna*), because it is the supreme imperishable (*paramākṣara*) free from the conceptualization of the perishable and the imperishable. (6–8). Because the Supreme Self has discarded the meanings of various words and sentences, and because it is devoid of the words and their referents such as "Being-Consciousness-Bliss" (*saccidānanda*) found in the great sentences, it cannot be pointed out. It becomes unapproachable by the Vedic statements within the scope of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*); thus, it is "one who goes where it cannot be reached" (*agamyaga*). (9–14).
Either there is the consequence that everything which is non-self is false, or [the view] "it is non-self" is [false], or even the mind [itself] is non-self. (15)
Determine that even the world is "not-self," for there is no such thing as a non-self;
this is because of the emptiness of all conceptual constructions and the abandonment of all purposeful activity. (16)
Determine with certainty that because there is nothing but Brahman alone, the non-self does not exist;
for it is devoid of the three bodies and free from the three periods of time. || 17 ||

Because of the absence of the qualities of the three living beings, because of the abandonment of the threefold suffering, because of being devoid of the three worlds, and because of the teaching that "the Self is everything," [it is so]. || 18 ||
Due to the absence of mind, there is nothing to be thought; due to the absence of a body, there is no old age.
Due to the absence of feet, there is no movement; due to the absence of hands, there is no action.
There is no death due to the absence of people; there is no pleasure and so forth due to the absence of cognition.
There is no dharma, no purity, no truth, and no fear.
There is no utterance of syllables, nor even the relationship of teacher and disciple;
in the absence of one, there is no second, and in the absence of the second, there is no oneness. (21)
If there were some reality, unreality could not possibly exist;
if unreality were to exist, reality would not be tenable. (22)
Know that what is auspicious may be inauspicious, and from the inauspicious, the auspicious is sought;
know that fear may be fearlessness, for indeed, from fearlessness, fear may arise. (23)
If there is bondage, there is liberation; in the absence of bondage, where is liberation?
If there is birth, there is death; in the absence of birth, there is no death. (24)
"I" would also exist as "you," and if there were no "you," then "I" would not exist at all;
if this [world] exists as that [Self], then in the absence of that, this does not exist either. (25)
If it exists, then it does not exist; if it does not exist, then something exists.
If there is an effect, there must be some cause; in the absence of an effect, there is no cause.
If there is duality, then there is non-duality; yet in the absence of duality, there is no "non-dual.
If there is an object of sight, then there is also the seer; but in the absence of the object of sight, there is no seer at all.
If reality exists internally, it does not exist externally; and if it is non-existent externally, it does not exist internally.
If there is any [aspect of] fullness, then a state of incompleteness necessarily follows. || 28 ||
Therefore, this—neither "you" nor "I," nor "these" nor "this"—does not exist anywhere.
There is no illustrative example for the Truth, and indeed, there is no thing to be illustrated in the Unborn.
The mind is certainly not the recollection that "I am the Supreme Brahman";
rather, this entire world is Brahman alone, and you as well as I are Brahman alone. (30)
Resolve with certainty: "I am pure consciousness alone; the non-self does not exist.
This phenomenal world does not exist at all; it has never arisen, nor does it abide anywhere. (31)
They say that the mind is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); it does not exist, it truly does not exist at any time.
There is no proliferation, no mind and so forth, no ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and no individual soul (*jīvaka*). || 32 ||
There is no effect of illusion and so forth, nor is there illusion; indeed, there is no fear.
There is no agent, no action, and neither hearing nor reflection.
The two types of concentration do not exist, nor indeed do the measures of a mother and so forth;
there is no ignorance at all, nor ever any lack of discernment.
There is neither the fourfold connection, nor indeed the threefold relationship; there is no Gaṅgā, no Gayā, no Setu, no past, nor does anything else exist. 35.
Neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air, nor space exists anywhere;
neither the gods, nor the guardians of the quarters, nor the Vedas, nor the Guru exist anywhere. (36)
It is neither distant nor near, neither gross nor medium, nor is it situated anywhere;
it is neither non-duality, nor is it the reality of duality, nor is it this unreality.
There is neither bondage nor liberation, neither existent nor non-existent, nor pleasure and the like;
there is no birth, no passing away, no caste, and nothing of the mundane world.

"Everything is Brahman"—this does not exist at all; nor indeed does "Brahman does not exist" exist. "It is only consciousness"—this does not exist at all; for there is no speaking of "I am consciousness. (39)
"I am Brahman; this does not exist at all. I am eternally pure, nowhere [defiled]. Whatever is spoken by speech, or whatever is thought by the mind anywhere—[all that is unreal]. (40)
One determines through the intellect that it does not exist, yet it is certainly not known by the mind;
there is no such thing as yoga or the like, nor is everything always existent, nor is it always non-existent.
There is no such thing as day and night, nor indeed bathing, meditation, and so forth;
there is neither delusion nor non-delusion—be certain that "no-self" does not exist. 42.
The Veda, the Śāstra, and the Purāṇa; the effect, the cause, and the Lord;
the world, the elements, and the people—all this is a unity, and everything is false; of this there is no doubt. (43)
Bondage, liberation, happiness, suffering, meditation, the mind, gods, and asuras—the secondary, the primary, the supreme, and all else—is entirely false; of this there is no doubt. (44)
Whatever is spoken by speech, whatever is imagined through volitions, and whatever is thought by the mind—all that is false; of this there is no doubt. (45)

Whatever is determined by the intellect, whatever is resolved within the mind, whatever is elaborated upon by the scriptures, and whatever is perceived by the eye alone—[all that is but the Self]. (46)
Whatever is heard with the two ears, as well as anything else that exists, the eye, the ear, and the body itself—these are firmly determined to be false. (47)
That which is pointed out as "this" is conceptualized as "this one"; likewise, "you," "I," "that," "this," "he," "I," "another," and even "existence"—all are thus conceived. (48)

Whatever is conceivable in the world, including the agitation of all mental constructs, all superimposition, all that is to be hidden, and the various distinctions of all enjoyments—[all this arises from it]. (49)
And all the various categories of defects consist in [the notion] "there is no self"; determine this. [Likewise,] "mine," "yours," "my own," and "your own" [are likewise to be understood]. (50)
Statements such as "for me," "for you," and "by me," and so forth, would all become false;
likewise, [claims] such as "Viṣṇu is the protector" and "Brahmā is the cause of creation" [would be false]. (51)
In the process of dissolution, everything is indeed Rudra; thus, resolve that all is illusory.
Bathing, recitation, austerity, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and the worship of the gods—[all these are likewise so]. (52)
Mantra and tantra, association with the virtuous, the manifestation of virtues and defects, the true nature of the internal organ, and the arising of ignorance. (53)
"Ascertain that the entire multitude of millions of world-systems is false;
for the word spoken by any teacher whatsoever has been so determined. (54)
Whatever is seen in the world, whatever is observed in the world, and whatever exists in the world—determine that all of it is false. (55)
Whatever has been spoken by anyone through any syllable, whatever has been determined by anyone, whatever has been uttered by anyone, and whatever has been rejoiced in by anyone— (56)
Whatever has been given by anyone, whatever has been done by anyone—wherever there is a virtuous deed and wherever there is a misdeed. (57)
Whatever you do with truth, determine it all to be false.

(p. 93) Regarding what was asked by Nidāgha—"Please explain the true nature of the Self and the non-Self"—the true nature of the Self (*ātmayāthātmya*) has been declared therein as this Self, which is established through the negation (*apahnava*) of the state of ignorance (*avidyāpada*) and its entire collection of effects, which are distinct from itself. Now, the true nature of the non-Self (*anātmayāthātmya*) is stated: "The non-Self. There is not even a report that the non-Self exists or does not exist. Since it might be thought that ignorance could exist in the form of ignorance, or in the form of its effect—the mind—or in the form of the waking state, [the text] says: "The non-Self" (verse 15). Even the world, which is the effect of the mind, does not exist. Because it is so, therefore, O Nidāgha, resolve with certainty: "There is no non-Self," whether in the form of cause and effect or in any other way. Be one who possesses this conviction: "Neither ignorance nor illusion exists here"; for those who investigate the reality of things, ignorance is merely the appearance of ignorance.
Those who know reality understand that this [world] is not by way of its own nature, nor is it different, nor in any way its own; it is neither separate nor non-separate.

Thus, according to the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and the teaching of Ācārya Gauḍapāda: he states three reasons for the impossibility of the world, the mind, and the non-Self (*anātman*)—beginning with "all" (*sarva*). Because of being devoid of all volitions (*saṃkalpa*), there is an absence of the mind which is possessed of thousands of functions such as volition; because of the abandonment of all effects, there is an absence of the world which is the effect of the mind. (16) Since Brahman alone exists as non-dual, and because the non-Self—which is the cause of the mind and its effects—is sublated, it is established that the non-Self does not exist; thus, be certain that "the non-Self does not exist. Furthermore, he sets forth the reasons for the impossibility of the non-Self beginning with "body" (*deha*). (17–20) Whatever is dependent is qualified, because it is the non-Self; whatever is not the non-Self is not qualified either, just like the non-qualified Brahman. Thus, by means of scripture and reasoning, he cites scriptural passages that are dependent [on their opposites] for the sake of establishing the Self alone, which is realized through the sublation of the non-Self imagined by oneself. (21–27) Regarding "end" (*anta*), there is a loss of the visarga, meaning "in the midst" (*antar*); regarding "existence" (*bhāva*), [there is a similar elision]. (28–30) But how is it said that the non-Self does not exist? Because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) of the non-Self is seen to possess origination, maintenance, and dissolution. To this he says: "this" (*idam*). While one should have said "this world" (*ayaṃ prapañcaḥ*), the change of gender in "this world" (*idaṃ prapañca*) is a grammatical anomaly. (31–36) It is not [possible to say] "between the far and the near," meaning there is no intervening space. Due to mutual dependence, there is no non-duality (*advaita*). (37–41) "Error" (*bhrānti*) is the perception of something as what it is not; "non-error" (*abhrānti*) is the perception of something as what it truly is. Some hold that in the phrase "there is no non-error" (*abhrāntir nāsti*), the visarga is dropped because the state of error and so forth is an effect of the ignorance of the subtle internal organ (*tūlāntaḥkaraṇa-avidyā*), and thus the cause and effect are identical. In that view: "error and non-error... (32) ...[and so on]. (33–41) He explains the nature of the non-Self through the illustration of a dream. The reading is "nāstyeva" (it does not exist at all). || 42 || He states with the words beginning "veda" that whatever is conceptualized by the vision of one who lacks self-knowledge (*svājña*), the knower of the Self (*svajña*) considers each of those to be false. The word "vedam" is an instance of the transposition of case endings (*vibhaktivyatyaya*). || 43–57 ||
I am the supreme self-nature of all things;
you alone are the supreme self, and you alone are the supreme teacher. (58)
You alone are of the nature of space; you are forever devoid of a witness.
You alone are all existence; you are Brahman, without a doubt. (59)
You are beyond time, you are Time itself; you are eternally Brahman, a mass of consciousness.
You are the essential nature of all things everywhere, and you possess a density of pure awareness.
You are truth, you are the perfected one, you are eternal, you are liberated, you are liberation, you are joy and immortality;
you are the god, you are peace, you are free from ailment, you are Brahman, you are the full, you are higher than the highest. (61)
You are equal, you are truth, you are eternal; you are awakened by such statements as "Thou art the Truth.
You are devoid of all limbs, yet you are ever-present; you are manifested as Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, and the other gods. || 62 ||

You are free from the delusion of all conceptual proliferation; you shine forth within all beings. You are everywhere devoid of volitional construction; you are realized as the ultimate meaning at the end of all scriptures.
Everywhere you are seated upon the throne of the bliss of contentment; everywhere you are devoid of movement and the like;
everywhere you are devoid of marks and the like; you are meditated upon incessantly by Viṣṇu and the other gods.
You are the very nature of the form of consciousness; you are pure consciousness alone, unrestrained.
You abide in the Self alone; you are entirely void and devoid of qualities.
You are bliss; you are the supreme; you alone are without a second.
You are the embodiment of the mass of consciousness and bliss, whose very nature is perfectly complete.
In the assembly you are the Knower; you are He who knows and beholds.
You are the embodiment of Existence-Consciousness-Bliss; you are indeed the Lord Vāsudeva.
You are the immortal and you are the all-pervading; you are indeed the restless and you are indeed the immovable.
You are the all, yet you are devoid of all; you are free from both the peaceful and the unpeaceful.
You are the manifestation of pure existence; for you are indeed the universal existence itself.
You are the nature of eternal perfection, yet you are devoid of all [worldly] accomplishments.
You are devoid of even the slightest measure of duality; you are free from even an atom of distinction.
You are devoid of existence, yet you are free from non-existence and all such categories.
You are devoid of both the characterized and the characteristics; you are changeless and free from affliction.
You are within all sounds, yet you are devoid of even the smallest divisions of time such as *kalā* and *kāṣṭhā*.
Devoid of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, you behold your own true nature;
you remain as nothing but your own true nature, submerged in the ocean of your own bliss.
In the kingdom of your own self, you are yourself, devoid of any objective existence;
you are the nature of the perfected and complete, and you see nothing other than yourself.
(96) You do not deviate from your own true nature; you expand through your own true nature.
You are indeed non-different from your own true nature; realize, "I am indeed [that]. 74.

Beginning with "The Veda is a scripture," up to this point in the text, it has been established that everything is false. Observing the doubt—"Am I included within that which is false?"—he says, "You alone [are the Self]," meaning that you are the Supreme Self, who is either the substratum of falsity or without any substratum, because he is the teacher of the knowledge of Brahman by virtue of being the very self of the Lord. (58–74)
The nature of the phenomenal world of ignorance and its effects is that of an absolute non-existence devoid of any counter-correlate:
"Whatever exists in this world, whatever constitutes this phenomenal expansion—whether in the form of the seen or the form of the seer—all is like the horn of a hare. (75)
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego, as well as energy, the world, and the circle of the universe. (76)
Destruction and birth, truth, merit, sin, victory, and so forth;
passion, desire, anger, greed, meditation, the object of meditation, and the supreme quality. (77)
The teacher, the disciple, the instruction, and so forth—from beginning to end—are auspicious tranquility;
they are the past, the future, and the present; they are the characterized, the characteristic, and non-duality.

Tranquility, discernment, contentment, and the forms of the eater and the eaten, as well as the eightfold yoga beginning with restraint (yama), which consists of coming and going—[these are the characteristics]. (79)

Hari and Śiva are to be grasped at the beginning, middle, and end, as well as within; likewise, the senses, the mind, and the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep] are to be abandoned. (80)
The twenty-four principles and the fourfold means of accomplishment—homogeneous and heterogeneous—are the worlds, beginning with the earth, in their respective order. (81)

The conduct of all castes and stages of life, the compendium of mantras, tantras, and so forth, as well as the nature of knowledge and ignorance, and all that is both insentient and sentient—[all this is contained within] the entire Veda. (82)
The distinction between bondage and liberation, consisting of knowledge and discernment; or the nature of awakening and non-awakening, and the discourse on duality and non-duality. (83)

The established conclusion of all Vedānta, the definitive determination of the meaning of all scriptures, the existence of many individual souls, and the resolution that [this] is determined from the perspective of the single soul (ekajīva). || 84 ||
Whatever one meditates upon with the mind, whatever is conceptualized anywhere, whatever is determined by the intellect, and whatever one hears from the teacher; || 85 ||
Whatever one articulates with speech, whatever is spoken by a teacher, whatever is experienced through one's own senses, and whatever is investigated individually—[all this is the Self]. (86)
Whatever has been determined according to reason by the great masters who have reached the further shore of the Vedas:
Śiva indeed destroys the worlds, and Viṣṇu protects the three worlds. (87)
Brahmā indeed creates the worlds, as well as such primary activities and so forth;
whatever exists in the Purāṇas and whatever is determined in the Vedas [is his work]. (88)
The essence of all the Upanishads is entirely like the horn of a hare.

O Master, by the power of your grace, I am now one whose nature is perfected and complete; of this there is no doubt. [I have realized] that previously experienced world-phenomenon—the expansion of the internal and external, consisting of the categories of the seer and the seen, and inflamed by the distinction between the individual (vyasti) and the collective (samasti), which is the state of one's own ignorance (svavidya) and its effects—is likewise so.

(p. 98) When the inquiry arises as to "what is its state?", he says "this" (idam) [verse 75]: although it is experienced as real from the perspective of one who does not know himself (*svājña-dṛṣṭi*) and as false from the perspective of one who knows himself (*svajña-dṛṣṭi*), from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), it is indeed of the nature of a non-existence that has no counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika-abhāva-rūpa*), like the horn of a hare. Thus, the negation (*apahnava*) of what is other than oneself has been stated; for there is no longer any object remaining to be negated. In response to the question, "For what purpose is the subsequent portion of the text commenced?", he says "the earth," etc. [verses 76–83]: It is true that there is no object for negation, because it is a non-entity (*avastu*) like the horn of a hare. Nevertheless, the commencement of the subsequent text is appropriate for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the Śruti passages beginning with "this phenomenal world" (*idaṃ prapañcam*) and ending with "like the horn of a hare. Verses 84–88 [explain that] the multiplicity of the ignorance (*avidyā*) within the subtle mind (*tūla-antaḥkaraṇa*) is the cause for the existence of multiple individual souls (*jīva*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it is meant that the duality of ignorance—the cause of both unity and multiplicity—is false from the perspective of the empirical level (*vyāvahārika*) and so forth. The meaning is that from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), it is entirely logical that anything distinct from Brahman is a non-entity, like the horn of a hare.
The mind itself, in the form of volition and so forth, is the cause of all misfortune;
that internal organ which conceives the volition "I am the body" is known as the mind (manas). (89)
The conception "I am the body" is called the great cycle of worldly existence;
the conception "I am the body" is also called its bondage. (90)
The thought "I am the body" is called its suffering;
that knowledge which says "I am the body" is remembered as hell itself. (91)
The notion "I am the body" is expressed as the entire world;
this conception "I am the body" is called the knot of the heart. (92)
The cognition that "I am the body" is itself called ignorance;
the cognition that "I am the body" is indeed a state of unreality. (93)
The notion that "I am the body" is called ignorance (avidyā);
the cognition that "I am the body" is itself termed duality (dvaita). || 94 ||
The conceptualization "I am the body" is indeed that very living being (jīva) as it exists in reality;
for that cognition which thinks "I am the body" is described as being limited. (95)
The thought "I am the body" is clearly a great sin; the notion "I am the body" is indeed thirst, a disease of defects. Whatever conceptualization there may be is said to be the threefold suffering.

Know, O gentle one, that desire, anger, bondage, all suffering, the entire web of defects, the various forms of time, and whatever this entire net of mental constructs is—all this is but the mind. (97)
The mind alone is the entire universe; the mind alone is the great enemy.
The mind indeed is saṃsāra; the mind alone is the three worlds. (98)
The mind alone is great suffering; the mind alone is old age and the like;
the mind indeed is time, and likewise, the mind is impurity.
For the mind alone is volition; the mind alone is the individual soul (jīvaka);
the mind alone is consciousness (citta), and the mind is indeed the ego (ahaṃkāra). || 100 ||
The mind alone is the great bondage; that mind is indeed the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
The mind alone is the earth, and the mind alone is the water. (101)
For the mind alone is fire, and the mind alone is the great wind;
the mind alone is space, and the mind alone is sound. 102.
Touch, form, taste, and smell—these five sheaths are born of the mind;
the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth, are said to be composed of the mind. (103)
The guardians of the quarters, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas are composed of mind;
the visible, insentient world of dualities is known as mental ignorance. (104)
Resolve that whatever is merely a mental construction (saṃkalpa), none of it exists;
the entire world does not exist, nor indeed do teacher, disciple, and so forth. 105.
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.

Anticipating the question, "What is the cause of these misfortunes that arise through the attachment to the vision of one's own ignorance? [the text] states that volition (*saṃkalpa*) alone is the cause of all misfortune—beginning with the verse on the "body" (*deha*). The change in case endings in the phrase "volition" (*saṃkalpam*) and so forth is for metrical reasons. (Verses 89–96) To the question, "What is the root of volition? [the text] replies, "Desire" (*kāma*) and so forth. (Verses 97–104) The meaning is that the state of one's own ignorance (*avidyā*), along with its entire collection of effects, is nothing other than the mind (*manas*). The word "Upaniṣad" indicates the conclusion of the chapter. (Verse 105)
Thus ends the fifth chapter. || 5 ||
The Sixth Chapter: The Reality, Consciousness, and Bliss of All.
Ribhu:
Know that everything consists of Being-Consciousness; everything is pervaded by Being-Consciousness.
It is non-dual Being-Consciousness-Bliss, the imperishable Being-Consciousness-Bliss. || 1 ||
Indeed, that which is pure Being-Consciousness-Bliss is other than Being-Consciousness-Bliss;
I am of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, and the void is indeed Being-Consciousness-Bliss.

"You are indeed Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda), and I am Being-Consciousness-Bliss. Whatever web of conceptualizations of names and forms is imagined by the vision of one’s own ignorance, all that, through the vision of one’s own true knowledge, consists of Being-Consciousness-Bliss. From the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha-dṛṣṭi), there is no possibility whatsoever of anything existing apart from Brahman alone. If, through the vision of one’s own ignorance and so forth, the notions of 'it exists' or 'it does not exist' arise, then that is merely unreal. When the negation of the unreal—which is other than oneself—is accomplished, nothing but the non-dual Brahman remains. To elaborate upon this, the sixth chapter begins with the words "Ṛbhu... (1-2).
The state of being Brahman belongs to all;
these [faculties]—mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness—are merely an aggregate.
Neither you, nor I, nor anyone else—everything is exclusively Brahman alone.
There is nowhere any speech, no word, no Veda, no syllable, and no insentient matter.
Neither middle, nor beginning, nor end; neither truth, nor a basis;
neither suffering, nor happiness, nor any existent state—such is my primordial nature.
Neither the body, nor the mouth, nor the nose, nor the tongue, nor the two palates;
neither the teeth and lips, nor the forehead, nor even inhalation and exhalation.
There is no sweat, bone, or flesh; no blood and no urine;
neither distance nor proximity; no limb, no belly, and no crown.
There is no movement of hands or feet, no scripture, and no teaching; there is no knower, no act of knowing, and no object of knowledge; nor are there the states of waking, dreaming, or deep sleep.
Beyond the fourth state (turyātīta), there is nothing of mine; everything is pervaded by the nature of Being-Consciousness (saccinmaya).
It is neither internal (adhyātmika), nor elemental (ādhibhūta), nor celestial (adhidaiva), nor illusory (māyika).
The wise one does not perceive the Taijasa, nor the Virāj, nor the Sūtra, nor the Īśvara;
there is no activity of coming and going, nothing lost, and no purpose [to be served]. 10.

p. 102) One should neither reject nor accept, nor find fault with, that which is pure or impure; likewise, one should not consider whether it is fat or lean, moist or dry, or its time and local dialect. (11)
There is no "all," no fear, no duality, and no trees, grass, or mountains;
there is no meditation, no perfection in yoga, and no [distinction between] Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas.
There is no bird, no beast, no woman, nor greed, nor delusion;
there is no pride, nor envy, nor likewise lust, anger, and the rest.
There are no women, Śūdras, or cats, nor any food such as what is fit to be chewed or eaten;
there are neither the elderly nor the young, no atheism, and indeed no opportunity for worldly talk.

There is neither the mundane nor the world, neither activity nor delusion; there is no enjoyer, no enjoyment, and no object of enjoyment, nor the triad of knower, means of knowledge, and object of knowledge. 15.
There is no enemy, friend, son, and so forth; no mother, no father, no sister; no birth, no death, no growth; and the delusion that "I am the body" does not exist. (16)
It is neither empty nor non-empty; there is no activity of the internal organ.
There is no night, no day, no night-time; there is no Brahmā, no Hari, and no Śiva.
Neither the days, fortnights, months, and so forth, nor the year, nor anything unstable;
neither the world of Brahmā, nor Vaikuṇṭha, nor Kailāsa, nor any other place [is eternal]. (18)
Neither heaven nor the Lord of the Gods, neither the world of Agni nor Agni himself;
neither Yama nor the world of Yama, nor the worlds or the world-protectors. || 19 ||
Neither the three worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, nor Pātāla, nor the surface of the earth;
neither ignorance nor knowledge, nor Māyā, nor inert Prakṛti. || 20 ||
There is neither permanence nor momentariness, neither destruction nor movement, nor running;
there is nothing to be meditated upon, no bathing for me, no mantra, and never any recitation. (21)
Neither a ritual substance, nor that which is worthy of worship, nor consecration, nor adoration;
neither flowers, nor fruit, nor leaves, nor incense such as perfumes and blossoms. || 22 ||
There is no hymn of praise, no prostration, not even the slightest circumambulation;
there is no prayer, no sense of separateness, no oblation, and no worship of the fire. (23)
There is neither sacrifice nor ritual acts, neither harsh speech nor eloquent discourse;
there is neither the Gāyatrī nor the twilight prayers, neither mental composure nor a state of distress. (24)
He is neither one of ill-hoped intent, nor of wicked soul, nor a Caṇḍāla, nor a Paulkasa;
he is neither one who is difficult to endure, nor one of harsh speech, nor a Kirāta, nor a deceiver.
He has neither partiality nor a partisan faction; he is free from vanity and the thief of ornaments; he is neither a hypocrite nor a pretender, and he is neither deficient nor superior as a man. (26)
It is not one, nor two, nor three, nor four; it is neither greatness nor smallness;
it is neither full nor limited; it is neither Kāśī, nor a vow, nor austerity.
There is no lineage, no family, no sūtra, no sovereign power, and no emptiness;
there is no woman, no female, no old woman, no maiden, and no state of being threadless. 28.
There is no impurity of birth nor the state of being born, nor the internal delusion;
there is neither the Great Saying (mahāvākya) nor oneness, nor the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā). || 29 ||
Because everything is pure consciousness alone, it is never subject to any defect whatsoever;
because everything is of the nature of pure existence, it consists solely of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda). || 30 ||
Brahman alone is everything; there is nothing else. I am that, I am that; likewise, I am indeed that, I am indeed that; I am the eternal Brahman. (31)
I am indeed Brahman, not a transmigrating being; I am indeed Brahman, I have no mind.
I am indeed Brahman, I have no intellect; I am indeed Brahman, and I have no sense organ.
I am Brahman alone, not the body; I am Brahman alone, not an object of perception;
I am Brahman alone, not the individual soul (jīva); I am Brahman alone, not a ground for duality.
I am Brahman alone; I am not inert matter. I am Brahman; death does not belong to me. I am Brahman alone; I am not the vital breath. I am Brahman alone, higher than the highest.
This is Brahman, the Supreme Brahman; He is the Truth, for He is the Lord.
Time is Brahman, the parts of time are Brahman, and bliss is Brahman, self-luminous.
Brahman is one, Brahman is two; delusion is Brahman, as are tranquility and the like.
Fault is Brahman, virtue is Brahman; self-restraint, peace, the all-pervading, and the Lord are Brahman.
The world is Brahman; the teacher is Brahman; the disciple is Brahman; Sadāśiva is Brahman.
The prior is Brahman, the supreme is Brahman; the pure is Brahman, as are the auspicious and the inauspicious. (37)
The individual soul is indeed always Brahman; "I am Existence-Consciousness-Bliss.
Everything is declared to be composed of Brahman; the entire universe is composed of Brahman. (38)
One is oneself Brahman, there is no doubt; nothing whatsoever exists apart from oneself.
All is indeed the Self, the pure Self; all is non-dual pure consciousness alone. (39)

"The Self, whose nature is eternally pure, is indeed nothing other than the Self; there is no mind and so forth apart from Brahman, which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss" (3-29). Beginning with "neither mind, nor intellect, nor ego" and ending with "the powers such as *aṇimā*," whatever has been superposed by the vision of one who does not know himself, and whatever has been negated by the vision of one who knows himself as being non-distinct from Brahman—all that [is sublated]—and so forth (30-39).
Brahman is the state of being one's own non-dual self alone;
this world is but a mere atom, its form existing as a mere atom. || 40 ||
Whether the body is the size of an atom, or indeed unreal as an atom, or inconceivable as an atom, or indeed conceivable as an atom. (41)
Brahman alone is everything; the three worlds are mere consciousness and nothing but Brahman.
It is bliss, supreme bliss; there is nothing else whatsoever.
Pure consciousness alone is the syllable Om; it is indeed Brahman itself, the totality.
I alone am the entire universe, and I alone am the supreme state.
I alone am beyond all qualities; I alone am higher than the highest;
I alone am the Supreme Brahman; I alone am the teacher of teachers. || 44 ||
I alone am the support of all; I alone am bliss beyond bliss.
There is no world other than the Self, nor is there any bliss other than the Self. 45.
There is no other goal than the Self; the entire world consists of the Self.
Indeed, there is nothing anywhere other than the Self; there is not even a blade of grass other than the Self.
There is no husk other than the Self; the entire world belongs to the Self.
All this is Brahman alone; it is not non-existent, for it is indeed Brahman alone. 47.
Everything heard is merely Brahman; it is itself only the absolute Brahman.
Everything encompassed is merely Brahman; it is merely Brahman, the essence and the bliss. 48.
(106) Only Brahman is the space of consciousness, existence-consciousness-bliss, and non-dual.
There is nothing other than Brahman, nor is there a world other than Brahman. 49.
There is nothing other than Brahman; indeed, there is no fruit other than Brahman.
There is no blade of grass other than Brahman; indeed, there is no state other than Brahman. (50)
There is no teacher other than Brahman; there is no unreal form other than Brahman;
and there is no sense of "I" other than Brahman—for indeed, neither "you-ness" nor "this-ness" exists anywhere apart from Him.
Know yourself to be of the nature of Brahman; there is nothing whatsoever other than yourself.
Whatever is seen in the world, and whatever is spoken by people—[know all that to be yourself]. (52)
Whatever is eaten anywhere is indeed entirely unreal—whether it be the difference of the agent, the difference of the action, the difference of qualities, or the taste and so forth. (53)
This entire diversity of gender is always non-existent and blissful;
so too are the distinctions of time, place, substance, victory, and defeat. (54)
Whatever diversity exists, all that is indeed nothing but non-existence;
the internal organ is non-existent, and the senses and so forth are likewise non-existent.
Everything beginning with the vital breaths is unreal; the aggregate is of an unreal nature. That which is called the five sheaths is unreal, and the five deities are unreal.
The six transformations and so forth are unreal; the host of enemies is unreal; the six seasons are indeed unreal, and likewise the six tastes are unreal. (57)
I am pure existence-consciousness-bliss; this world is unproduced.
I am the Self alone, the supreme reality; there are no other perceptions of worldly existence. (58)
(107) Truly, I am of the nature of bliss; my form is the solid mass of consciousness and bliss.
I alone am supreme bliss; I alone am higher than the highest. || 59 ||
All this has the form of consciousness; I am non-dual bliss of consciousness.
I am the nature of all illumination; I am the essential nature of the absence of all [duality]. (60)
The notion that "I alone am always the enjoyer" is unreal, arising from some source;
whereas "Thou" is the Supreme Brahman, whose nature consists of consciousness and bliss. (61)
The form of consciousness, the space of consciousness, consciousness itself is the supreme bliss.
I am indeed the Self; I am non-existent as a limited ego, I am the immutable, the supreme Guru.
I am pure existence-consciousness-bliss; this world is unproduced.
There is no time, there is no world, and even the primordial nature (prakṛti) of illusion does not exist.
I alone am Hari manifest; I alone am Sadāśiva.
I am the state of pure consciousness, the realization of pure being.
I am solely non-dual bliss; I am the single essence of the mass of consciousness.
Everything is eternally Brahman alone; everything is exclusively Brahman.
Everything is eternally Brahman alone; everything is Brahman alone as consciousness.
I am the inner ruler of all, characterized by being the witness of all.
I am the Supreme Self, the supreme light, the supreme abode, and the supreme goal; I am the essence of all Vedānta, well-established by all the scriptures.
I am the very nature of the bliss of yoga, the great manifestation of supreme bliss;
I am the illumination of all knowledge, the embodiment of primary consciousness.
I am the light of the fourth beyond the fourth, devoid of even the fourth beyond the fourth and so forth;
I am the imperishable consciousness, I am the Truth, Vāsudeva, ageless and immortal. (69)
I am Brahman, the space of consciousness, the eternal, stainless Brahman— pure, awakened, forever liberated, nameless, and formless.
I am of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss; this world is unarisen.
The world, whether real or unreal, does not exist, nor do mental constructs, imaginations, and the like.
Brahman is eternally composed of bliss, absolute, self-existent at all times,
infinite, immutable, peaceful, uniform, and free from ailment.

He describes the limited nature of the world—which is imagined by the vision of one's own ignorance as something separate from Brahman—the threefold absence of limitation in Brahman, which is its substrate, the negation of any generality other than Brahman in reality, and the fact that Brahman is non-dual pure Self alone, with the verse beginning "aṇumātra" (40–46). He states that the world is nothing but Brahman, which is non-dual and established through the negation of the unreal phenomenal expansion imagined by the ignorant, with the verse "brahmamātram idam" (47). He elaborates on this very point with the passage beginning "brahmamātraṃ śrutam" (48–71). To the question of what kind of thing this absolute Brahman is, he says: "anantam" (72).
The phenomenal world, which is other than myself, is non-existent; if it were anything other than me, it would be false, like a mirage in the desert.
If there were any fear whatsoever in the words of a barren woman’s son, [then this world might exist]. (73)
If the lord of serpents were to die by means of a rabbit’s horn, then this world would exist;
if one were to be satiated by drinking the water of a mirage, then let this world exist. (74)
If someone were destroyed by a human horn, let this [world] indeed exist; for if the city of the Gandharvas were real, the world would always be so. (75)
If the blueness in the sky were real, the world would be real; if the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell were real, the world would be a true ornament. (76)
If a man were bitten by a rope-snake, let there be worldly existence;
yet when the world is destroyed by the golden arrow in the blazing fire, [what remains]? (77)
If there were milk-rice in the Vindhya forest, the world would come into being;
once the cooking is perfected with a plantain-stalk for fuel, the world would arise. (78)

If the world were to come into being when the cooking is completed by means of forms that are immediately youthful, then let this world exist, just as the destruction of darkness occurs through lamps depicted in a painting. (79)
If a mortal who died a month ago were to return, the world would indeed exist;
if buttermilk were ever to take on the form of milk, the world might perhaps be eternal. (80)
May the milk produced from the udder serve for the re-establishment of the world; and may the dust of the earth, once arisen in the ocean, ensure the perpetual existence of the universe. 81.
If an elephant were bound by a hair from a tortoise's tail, let the world be overwhelmed by that;
if Mount Meru were moved by a thread situated on a lotus stalk, then the world might come to pass [as you claim]. (82)
If the ocean were bound by a garland of waves, let this world remain so;
if fire were to burn below, let the world always be thus. (83)
If a blazing fire were cool, and if this world existed in form;
if a lotus were to grow within a circle of blazing fire, then let this world exist. (84)
(110) Even if this world were to become a great sapphire from the king of mountains, or if Mount Meru were to come and stand within the lotus-eye—this would still be this very world. (85)
If the son of Bhṛṅga were to swallow Meru, or if this Meru were to move, or if a lion were killed by a gnat—only then would your word be true. (86)
If the three worlds were to exist within the vast expanse of a minute atom, and if the fire of grass were eternal, then the world would be momentary. (87)
If an object seen in a dream were to exist in the waking state, or if the current of a river were ever motionless, then by some means this world might come to be [real]. (88)
If fire were prepared as food for one who is hungry, or if the realm of jewels were always perfectly known by those born blind, then the world would be so. (89)
If the world were to experience the pleasure of women through a eunuch boy, or if there were a chariot constructed from the horn of a hare, then the world would truly exist. (90)
If a maiden who has just been born were to become fit for enjoyment in this world, or if a barren woman were to obtain the bliss of conception—only then could this world be known as such. (91)
Or let a crow move like a swan, or let the world become motionless;
or let a great donkey fight with a lion—if such were the state of the world. (92)
If the great donkey were to attain the gait of an elephant, let the world be so;
if the full moon and sun were to become dull by themselves, let the world shine [in that state]. (93)
If the world were visible even when Rāhu is seen after the moon, the sun, and so forth have been abandoned, and if there were growth from a fried seed, then let the world be real. (94)
Then the world will experience happiness, with the poor enjoying the wealth of the rich;
it will be so when the lion is defeated by the prowess of dogs. (95)
If the heart of the wise were known by the ignorant, it would then be a mere mental construction—like the thought that a dog has drunk the entire ocean without remainder. (96)
If pure space were to fall among human beings,
then the world would be like the sky fallen upon the earth— a fragrant flower of the sky.
When the pure space has become a forest and the world is always moving, there is no reflection of that world in the solitary mirror. (98)
The world does not exist within the belly of a goat, nor indeed does the world exist within one's own belly;
in every respect, the conceptualization of difference—whether as duality or non-duality—is not found.
If this differentiation is a product of illusion, then there is the contemplation of Brahman;
if there is the suffering of "I am the body," then there must be the certainty that "I am Brahman. (100)
When the knot of the heart exists, when it is being severed, and when doubt has arisen regarding the Wheel of Brahman, one shall attain certainty concerning Brahman. || 101 ||
If there is protection of the jewel of the Self from the thief that is the non-self form, then Brahman alone is eternally composed of bliss, existing by itself at all times. (102)

If there were the consequence of multiple distinctions such as delimitation, exhaustion, and calculation, then that which is characterized by various qualifiers such as "infinite" would not exist in reality. If there is the delusion that there exists a qualifier such as "infinite" apart from Me, [it is merely an illusion].

(p. 112) Then he says, "from Me," [meaning] that this [world] is indeed non-existent. But how can the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is perceived in many ways—as "the pot exists," "the cloth exists," and so forth—be absolutely non-existent? To address this doubt, since the perception "it exists" is nothing but Being (*sanmātra*), and because it is the non-dual Brahman alone, free from all counter-correlates (*niṣpratiyogika*), the possibility of a world distinct from oneself is impossible therein. Thus, mocking the reality of the universe through various examples such as "let this world be like the son of a barren woman," he reveals its unreality with the verse beginning "the barren woman... (vv. 73–78). The meaning is: "Let this world exist from the perspective of ultimate reality" (vv. 79–85). A mountain at the edge is a "nigiri. (vv. 86–88). "Agni-bhojya" is a case of elision of the *visarga*. (vv. 89–90). Regarding the term "sadyaḥ-kumārikā" (an instantaneously born girl), if one objects that there would be a tautology with "a girl who has just been born" (*sadyojātā*), it is not so; for just as there is a difference in words, there may be a difference in meaning. How so? By the statement "when cooking is accomplished by means of fuel in the form of 'instantaneous girls,' which are specific medicinal herbs renowned in medical science (*vaidya-śāstra*)," a specific kind of fuel for the act of cooking is indicated. Because a girl is constantly moist due to being filled with water, even if she were cast into the midst of a fierce fire, she would extinguish the fire; thus, there is no repetition, as cooking cannot be performed by her. (vv. 91–98). If it is argued that this world, characterized by distinctions such as the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and the collective (*samaṣṭi*), cannot be denied because it exists within the belly of the Cosmic Egg (*ajaka-kukṣi*)—that is, within the belly of the individual living beings of the collective world—and therefore does not deserve the status of non-existence, [the author] replies that it does not exist even in the three periods of time, with the word "aja" (unborn/egoless). The meaning is that since dualistic and non-dualistic functions, which appear through the perspectives of the ignorant and the wise respectively, are impossible from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no conceptualization of anything other than oneself within one’s own Self alone. (v. 99). Nevertheless, one must constantly practice the contemplation of Brahman; hence he says "Māyā. If duality exists from the perspective of the ignorant, from the perspective of the wise this world does not exist, but rather "this is Brahman alone"; thus, one must cultivate the realization of Brahman. For from the perspective of ultimate reality, neither of those two exists. Similarly regarding "I am the body" (vv. 100–101). In reality, it is Brahman consisting of eternal bliss, the absolute non-dual Brahman alone, free from all counter-correlates. (v. 102)
The method of contemplation, "I am Brahman," and other such excellent illustrations have established that only Brahman exists.
Since Brahman alone is the manifestation of all worlds, abandon the notion of a "world" as such. (103)
Having ascertained "I am Brahman" and having abandoned the sense of ego, everything indeed goes to dissolution, like a flower held in the hand of one who is asleep. (104)
There is neither body nor actions; everything is solely Brahman alone.
There is no element, no effect, and no fourfold state.
The cognition of the three characteristics is entirely nothing but Brahman alone; having abandoned all activity, meditate thus: "I am Brahman. (106)
"I am Brahman, there is no doubt; I am indeed Brahman, whose nature is consciousness.
Having ascertained that 'I am solely Being-Consciousness-Bliss,' abandon that [duality]. (107)
"Thus, etc."—in this Upaniṣad:
"Pure consciousness alone, pure consciousness which is the indivisible single essence, the essence devoid of all else;
pure consciousness free from everything is Brahman alone, for it is not non-existent."

The Śruti, considering the meaning thus declared by such passages—that one’s own nature alone is established through the negation (*apahnava*) of everything other than oneself—to be difficult to comprehend, repeatedly introduces relevant contexts so that the knowledge of Brahman alone, established through the negation of all else, may arise. Starting from the *Tejobindu Upaniṣad* and continuing through the fifteenth chapter, it first establishes the true nature of indivisible, pure Consciousness (*akhaṇḍa-śuddha-caitanya*) through intermediate verses accompanied by the yoga of the fifteen limbs of knowledge. Then, when the possibility arises—through the perspective of the ignorant—that the insentient world of objects, from its various states up to heaven, might be fragmented, the text reveals, in the form of a dialogue between Kumāra and Śiva, that "the visible is the indivisible single essence" (*akhaṇḍaikarasaṃ dṛśyam*) up to "everything is the indivisible single essence" (*akhaṇḍaikarasaṃ sarvam*), thereby demonstrating that "one is oneself the indivisible single essence. Next, when there is the possibility that things denoted by words such as "this" and "that" are merely insentient matter (*acinmātra*), it declares the nature of non-dual Consciousness devoid of any counterpart (*niṣpratiyogika-cinmātra-svarūpa*) with the passage beginning, "Whatever exists, whether something or nothing, is indeed only Consciousness. When the possibility of a dual Brahman arises, it states that "Brahman, which is the indivisible single essence, does not differ from Consciousness alone," thus expressing the convergence on a single meaning for both the indivisible single essence and Consciousness alone. Then, starting with "I am the Supreme Brahman," it reveals its own experience by demonstrating the unreality of the phenomenal world apart from itself. After praising the greatness of the mantra "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), it establishes that this truth is to be grasped by millions of seekers of liberation. Finally, under the guise of revealing the primary intermediate fruits, it begins with "I am the conscious Self" (*cidātmāham*) and "I am the Supreme Self" (*parātmāham*).

(p. 114) Having first revealed *jīvanmukti*—the fruit intermediate to the knowledge of the non-dual (*nirviśeṣa*)—with the passage ending, "He shall sleep in his own true nature; he is called one liberated while living"; and having then revealed *videhamukti*, characterized by abiding in That alone as the primary fruit of the knowledge of Brahman-only, beginning with "Becoming Brahman, with a perfectly tranquil self... and ending with "...rejoice in your own Self alone, O Vaidehī, you have reached liberation"; and further, resorting to another narrative, having established the true nature of the Self with "Brahman is the limit of all speech... and the true nature of the non-Self with "The notion that there is a 'non-Self'... etc.; and having weakened the notion of duality and plurality resulting from the mention of both Self and non-Self—using scriptural reasonings such as "in the absence of one, there is no second"—by showing that in various places the Self and non-Self, though distinct in word and meaning, are in reality one's own Self alone, which is a state of existence devoid of any counterpart; and by using the example of the absolute impossibility of a world external to oneself—such as "if there were fear at the words of a barren woman’s son" or "like a hare’s horn, it is of the nature of absolute non-existence"—even disregarding grammatical changes in case, gender, and person as if they were forgotten; because this Śruti proceeds without repetition (*jāmitā*), no suspicion of redundancy can stand in this entire collection of Vedānta scriptures. For the Śruti, which has attained the state of being nothing but one's own ignorance, is occupied with the coronation ceremony for the sovereignty of *vikalebara-kaivalya* (liberation while in the body), characterized by the remainder of Brahman-only, which is established through the negation of the delusion regarding whether anything exists or does not exist apart from its own continuum. Therefore, the wise should not recall any fault here. In the present context: if you are a seeker (*adhikārī*), then first contemplate that Brahman alone is the abode of all and the substratum of all. Then, abandon even the delusion of being a substratum defined by the objects superimposed upon it. (103) Having resolved "I am everything, I am Brahman," abandon the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) residing therein. If you are thus diligent, then whatever is imagined by you, all that is indeed [Brahman]. (104) At that time, there is no body... etc. (105). [This refers to] the *jahad-lakṣaṇā* (indication by abandoning part of the meaning). First, [abandon] all activity. (106) Abandon even that certainty, because even that mental modification (*vṛtti*) must be abandoned as something separate from the Self. As it has been said: [The verse continues: "Just as a snake is cast off from its slough, so is the body cast off by the yogi. Just as a bird leaves a nest, so the knower of Truth abandons the body. Thus, having abandoned the body, the senses, and the mind, one remains as the Self alone, free from all attributes. This is the state of the supreme non-dual realization. Therefore, the wise should not entertain any doubt regarding the consistency of these teachings. (Note: The provided text contains a mix of commentary and verses. The translation above focuses on the philosophical exposition and the core instructions.)
At that time, one who is devoid of the memory of the body and the Videha state— if even a slight remembrance [of the previous stage] occurs, then he becomes endowed with everything.
Thus [ends the verse]. 107.
The rule for the transmission of the scripture:
this great Śaṅkara-scripture is not to be given to just anyone—not to an atheist, nor to an ungrateful person, nor to one of evil conduct, nor to one of wicked soul. (108)
Having thoroughly examined him for one month, six months, or a year, it should be given to that great-souled one whose inner heart is purified by devotion to the Guru.
Having respectfully cast aside the study of all other Upanishads from afar,
one should always joyfully practice the Tejobindu Upanishad.
By mere single practice, one becomes Brahman oneself;
"one becomes Brahman oneself"—this is the Upaniṣad. 111.

Revealing the meaning of the tradition of the scriptures (*śāstra-saṃpradāya*), he concludes with the words "Śāṅkarīyam. To the question of to whom it should not be given and to whom it should be given, he says: "There is none" (*nāsti*). (108–110) Thus, one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*) and has obtained knowledge from the mouth of the Guru should abandon the practice of all other *Upaniṣads*. To the question of what is gained by abandoning everything and practicing this alone, he says: "Once" (*sakṛt*). The meaning is that by merely hearing or reading it once, the wise person remains as the non-dual Brahman alone, which is established through the negation of everything else (*sarvāpahnavasiddha*). The word "Upaniṣad" marks the conclusion of the *Tejobindu Upaniṣad*. (111)
Thus ends the sixth chapter. || 6 ||
This clear and concise commentary on the *Tejobindu* has been written by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
The extent of the commentary on the Tejobindu Upaniṣad is recorded as seven hundred and fifty-four [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Tejobindu Upaniṣad, completing the thirty-seventh [treatise] in the exposition of the scripture consisting of one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Īśa.
